The module aims to develop a solid understanding of text mining and NLP fundamentals, including text preprocessing and vector representations of text. Students learn how language models evolved into transformers and modern large language model (LLM) architectures, and study both traditional and state-of-the-art approaches to core NLP tasks. A team project asks students to develop and apply a range of NLP methods to extract information and meaning from large-scale textual data.

Text mining and natural language processing have different historical emphases. Natural Language Processing (NLP) has traditionally focused on modelling linguistic structure and meaning, such as syntax, semantics, and discourse. Text mining has traditionally focused on discovering patterns and useful information from large text collections, for example topic modelling that groups documents into abstract themes without predefined definitions. In recent years the two fields have converged: they share representations, models, and evaluation benchmarks, overlap strongly in statistical and neural language processing, and modern large language models blur the distinction between them almost entirely.

Text mining and NLP power a wide range of everyday and specialist applications. Machine translation systems such as Google Translate convert text between languages. Question answering underlies voice assistants such as Amazon Alexa, which answer spoken questions and act on requests. Automated fact checking flags misleading claims on social platforms. Human language is hard to process for several reasons. Natural languages evolve constantly, with new words such as 'emoji' or new usages such as 'to DM' appearing all the time. Second, they enable document retrieval, where documents relevant to a query are returned, as in web search. Third, they

page_content: A vector, also called an embedding, is a one-dimensional array of d elements or coordinates, each identified by an index. A collection of n such vectors forms a matrix X of size n by d, which is also called a vector space; each row is a vector and each column is a coordinate or dimension. For text, the interesting question is what the rows and columns should represent. Note a common practical gotcha: in mathematics vector indices often start at 1, but in Python they start at

page_content: common practical gotcha: in mathematics vector indices often start at 1, but in Python they start at 0, so X[2, 1] refers to the third row and second column.

page_content: To measure how close two vectors are we use similarity functions. The dot product, or inner product, takes two equal-length vectors and returns a single number by summing the products of their matching coordinates. A drawback of the raw dot product is that it grows with vector length, so a document that is simply ten times longer than another, but about the same topic, can score a larger dot product purely because of its magnitude. Cosine similarity fixes this by normalising

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: larger dot product purely because of its magnitude. Cosine similarity fixes this by normalising the dot product, dividing by the two vectors' lengths (their magnitude or norm). This measures the angle between the vectors rather than their size, so it is invariant to document length and is the similarity measure used throughout this course.

page_content: There are two classic ways to lay out text as a matrix, differing in what the rows and columns mean. In a word-word or term-context matrix, both rows and columns are words, and each cell records how often a target word co-occurs with a context word; this captures word meaning. In a document-word or bag-of-words matrix, rows are documents and columns are vocabulary words, and each cell records how often a word appears in a document; this captures document content. Choosing the

page_content: cell records how often a word appears in a document; this captures document content. Choosing the layout is the first design decision when representing text, because it fixes what similarity between two rows will actually mean.

page_content: Before building a matrix we must fix the unit of text. A word, also called a token or term, is a sequence of one or more characters excluding whitespace, and can sometimes be an n-gram, a contiguous sequence of several words. A document, also called a text sequence or snippet, is any chosen span: a sentence, paragraph, section, chapter, whole document, search query, social media post, transcribed utterance, or a pseudo-document such as all tweets posted by one user. The

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: media post, transcribed utterance, or a pseudo-document such as all tweets posted by one user. The definitions of word and document are choices the designer makes, and they determine what the rows of the matrix are.

page_content: Tokenisation is the step that turns raw text into tokens. In its simplest form it splits text on whitespace or uses regular expressions to separate words and punctuation. For example, the raw sentence 'As far as I'm concerned, this is Lynch at his best.' becomes the token sequence 'As', 'far', 'as', 'I'm', 'concerned', ',', 'this', 'is', 'Lynch', 'at', 'his', 'best', '.'. Tokenisation is the foundation of the pipeline because every later step, from counting to weighting,

page_content: Tokenisation is the foundation of the pipeline because every later step, from counting to weighting, operates on the tokens it produces.

page_content: After tokenisation, several optional normalisation steps may follow: lowercasing, removal of punctuation, numbers, stop words, and infrequent words, and stemming, which reduces words to a common root. For instance, lowercasing and removing punctuation and stop words turns the tokens of a movie review into a compact bag such as 'concerned lynch best lost highway dark violent surreal beautiful hallucinatory masterpiece'. These steps shrink the vocabulary and strip out

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: violent surreal beautiful hallucinatory masterpiece'. These steps shrink the vocabulary and strip out uninformative high-frequency words so that the remaining counts carry more signal, though they also discard information and so are choices to make deliberately.

page_content: Given a corpus D of m pre-processed texts, such as a set of movie reviews or tweets, the vocabulary V is the set of all k unique words that appear in D. The vocabulary is often extended to include n-grams, contiguous sequences of n words, so that short phrases can be represented as single features. The size of the vocabulary, written |V|, sets the dimensionality of the discrete representations built on top of it, which is why vocabulary construction has a direct effect on how

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: representations built on top of it, which is why vocabulary construction has a direct effect on how large and how sparse the resulting matrices will be.

page_content: The simplest way to represent a word is a discrete one-hot vector. Given a vocabulary, each word is a vector the length of the vocabulary with a single 1 at the word's own index and 0 everywhere else. For the vocabulary {apple, apricot, chocolate, love, pie, pineapple} of size six, 'apricot' becomes [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0] and 'pineapple' becomes [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]. This encoding is easy to build but, as the next section shows, it throws away all information about how words relate

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: easy to build but, as the next section shows, it throws away all information about how words relate to one another.

page_content: One-hot vectors treat every word as equally different from every other word. Because each word has its single 1 at a unique index and 0 everywhere else, any two distinct one-hot vectors are orthogonal, so their dot product, and therefore their cosine similarity, is exactly 0. For 'apricot' = [0,1,0,0,0,0] and 'pineapple' = [0,0,0,0,0,1] the dot product is 0 even though the two fruits are clearly related. The representation captures no similarity at all, which motivates using

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: fruits are clearly related. The representation captures no similarity at all, which motivates using the contexts in which words appear to bring related words closer together.

page_content: The distributional hypothesis, associated with J. R. Firth's 1957 slogan 'You shall know a word by the company it keeps', states that words appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. It changes representation from assigning independent arbitrary IDs to words toward encoding each word by the contexts it keeps, so that words with similar neighbours sit close together in the vector space. The classic illustration is the unknown word 'tesguino': from sentences

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: together in the vector space. The classic illustration is the unknown word 'tesguino': from sentences such as 'A bottle of tesguino is on the table', 'Everybody likes an ice cold tesguino', 'Tesguino makes you drunk', and 'We make tesguino out of corn', the surrounding words let you infer that tesguino is an alcoholic drink made from corn, without ever consulting a dictionary.

page_content: A word-word or term-context matrix X has size n by m, where n is the number of target words and m the number of context words; usually the two vocabularies are the same, giving a square matrix. Each cell counts how often a target word co-occurs with a context word, measured within a context window of plus or minus k words to the left and right of the target, and accumulated over a large corpus such as the whole of Wikipedia. Under this representation, words that share

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: over a large corpus such as the whole of Wikipedia. Under this representation, words that share contexts end up with similar rows. In the lecture example, once counts are gathered, apricot and pineapple have cosine similarity 1 while apricot and digital have cosine similarity 0, which is exactly the behaviour the distributional hypothesis predicts.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: The notion of context can be refined using linguistic information rather than a plain window of neighbouring words. One option is to distinguish contexts by part-of-speech, so that the verb sense of 'bank' and the noun sense of 'bank' contribute to different counts. Another is to use syntactic dependencies, so that the direct-object context of 'eat' is kept separate from its subject context. Richer context definitions can produce vectors that reflect finer distinctions in how

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: subject context. Richer context definitions can produce vectors that reflect finer distinctions in how words are actually used.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: A document-word matrix X has size |D| by |V|, where rows are documents in the corpus and columns are vocabulary words. Each cell counts how many times a word appears in a document, so a row is the bag-of-words vector for that document; for example one document might have counts of 14 for 'bad', 1 for 'good', 0 for 'great', and 5 for 'terrible'. Equivalently, a document vector can be obtained by summing the one-hot vectors of all the words in the document. This representation

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: be obtained by summing the one-hot vectors of all the words in the document. This representation captures which words a document contains but, being a bag, it ignores the order in which they appear.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Raw co-occurrence and bag-of-words counts have a serious flaw: frequent words such as articles and pronouns dominate the vectors without being informative. Because a word like 'the' appears alongside almost every noun, its enormous counts swamp the rare but meaningful words. In the lecture example, adding 'the' to the contexts pushes the cosine similarity between the unrelated words 'apricot' and 'digital' up to 0.997, a spurious result driven entirely by the shared

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: unrelated words 'apricot' and 'digital' up to 0.997, a spurious result driven entirely by the shared high-frequency term. The same distortion affects the document-word matrix. The fix is to weight the vectors so that informative words count for more and ubiquitous words count for less.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: One way to weight a word-word matrix is distance discounting: context words are weighted according to how far they sit from the target word, so nearer context words count for more and farther ones count for less. For a window of plus or minus k, the context word at each position is multiplied by (k minus distance) divided by k. With k equal to 3, for example, the multipliers running outward from the target are 3/3, 2/3, and 1/3 on each side. This encodes the intuition that

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: running outward from the target are 3/3, 2/3, and 1/3 on each side. This encodes the intuition that immediate neighbours are usually more relevant to a word's meaning than distant ones.

page_content: Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) weights a word pair by how often two words occur together relative to how often they would occur if they were independent, computed as the base-2 logarithm of the joint probability divided by the product of the marginal probabilities. Positive PMI values quantify genuine relatedness, so PMI is used in place of raw counts. The problem is negative and undefined values: when two words never co-occur their joint probability is zero and the

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: negative and undefined values: when two words never co-occur their joint probability is zero and the logarithm of zero is undefined (tending to minus infinity), and unreliable negative scores arise for rare pairs. Positive PMI (PPMI) resolves this by clamping every value at a floor of zero, taking the maximum of the PMI and 0, which keeps the vectors well defined and non-negative.

page_content: TF-IDF weights the importance of a word in a document relative to a whole corpus by combining two factors. Term Frequency (TF) rewards words that appear often in a document, on the grounds that they are likely important to it. Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) penalises words that appear in many documents, on the grounds that they are poor at distinguishing one document from another; it is computed as the base-10 logarithm of N divided by df_w, where N is the number of

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: another; it is computed as the base-10 logarithm of N divided by df_w, where N is the number of documents and df_w is the number of documents containing the word. If a word appears in every one of the N documents, then N divided by df_w equals 1, and the logarithm of 1 is 0, so its IDF is 0 and its overall TF-IDF weight collapses to 0 no matter how frequent it is within a document. The final weight multiplies the term frequency by this IDF.

page_content: Count-based matrices for words and documents often work well but suffer from two related problems. They are high-dimensional, because the vocabulary can run to millions of words, and they are very sparse, because any one word co-occurs with only a small number of others and any one document contains only a tiny subset of the vocabulary, so most entries are zero. High-dimensional sparse vectors are computationally inefficient and awkward for many machine learning models. The

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: sparse vectors are computationally inefficient and awkward for many machine learning models. The solution is dimensionality reduction, which compresses the sparse high-dimensional matrix into a much smaller number of dense dimensions while preserving most of the useful structure.

page_content: Word vectors are evaluated in two complementary ways. Intrinsic evaluation tests the geometry of the vectors directly: ordering word pairs by semantic similarity, substituting a word in context without changing meaning, or solving analogy puzzles such as 'Beijing is to China as Rome is to ...?'. Extrinsic evaluation instead plugs the vectors into a separate downstream task, such as sentiment classification or named entity recognition, and judges the vectors by how much they

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: as sentiment classification or named entity recognition, and judges the vectors by how much they improve performance on that external application. So running vectors through a downstream sentiment classifier is an extrinsic evaluation, whereas an analogy puzzle is an intrinsic one.

page_content: Which word vectors are best is not simply a matter of high-dimensional count-based versus low-dimensional learned vectors. A later lecture shows how neural networks produce low-dimensional vectors, but Levy and colleagues (2015) found that hyperparameter choices, such as context window size and rare-word removal, often matter more than the choice of method itself. The choice of texts used to gather the counts also matters: more text is generally better, and low-dimensional

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: texts used to gather the counts also matters: more text is generally better, and low-dimensional methods scale better to large corpora.

page_content: Static word vectors have several limitations. Polysemy is one: all occurrences and all senses of a word are collapsed into a single vector, so the river sense and the financial sense of 'bank' share one coordinate and must be adapted per task to recover the intended sense. Antonyms are another: opposites such as 'hot' and 'cold' appear in very similar contexts, so they end up with similar vectors and are hard to tell apart from synonyms. Compositionality is a third: it is

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: with similar vectors and are hard to tell apart from synonyms. Compositionality is a third: it is unclear how to combine word vectors into the meaning of a phrase, and while simple combinations such as adding or multiplying vectors, or models such as sentence-BERT, work for short spans, they do not scale cleanly to whole sentences and paragraphs.

page_content: Language modelling is the first natural language processing problem introduced in this course. The central question it answers is: what is the probability of a given sequence of words in a particular language, such as English? At first glance assigning a probability to a sentence looks like an odd thing to want, but this single quantity turns out to underpin a surprising number of practical applications. A model that can tell us how likely a sequence of words is gives us a

of practical applications. A model that can tell us how likely a sequence of words is gives us a principled way to compare competing interpretations of text or speech and to prefer the one the language itself makes most plausible. This lecture builds on the previous session on vector representations of text and develops language models from simple word counts up to smoothed n-gram models.

Language models power many everyday tools. In information retrieval they estimate word likelihood for query completion: as you type 'Is Manchester' into a search engine, the model proposes the most probable continuations. In grammatical error detection they help decide between confusable alternatives such as 'You're welcome' versus 'Your welcome' by scoring which sequence is more probable. In speech recognition they disambiguate acoustically similar phrases: 'I scream is

probable. In speech recognition they disambiguate acoustically similar phrases: 'I scream is delicious' and 'Ice cream is delicious' sound almost identical, and the language model prefers the sequence that is more likely in ordinary English. Across all of these tasks the same idea recurs: score candidate word sequences and keep the most probable one.

The traditional artificial intelligence approach to language tries to find the interpretation of a sentence that is grammatical, semantically sensible, and pragmatically plausible in context. It does this by building explicit models of the rules that describe how language works. In practice this approach performs poorly in the real world. Wide-coverage rule systems are hard to maintain, and capturing semantics requires an enormous amount of hand-coded knowledge. These

to maintain, and capturing semantics requires an enormous amount of hand-coded knowledge. These limitations motivated the shift toward statistical methods that learn patterns from data rather than encoding them by hand.

Statistical approaches abandon explicit models of grammar, meaning, and context. Instead of encoding rules by hand, they collect statistics from data: how often different words appear, how often pairs or triples of words appear next to each other, and other more complex patterns of co-occurrence. These statistics are then used directly to perform NLP tasks such as speech recognition, text prediction, and translation. The appeal is that the same counting machinery generalises

text prediction, and translation. The appeal is that the same counting machinery generalises across tasks and scales with the amount of available text, avoiding the brittleness of hand-built rule systems.

N-gram statistics record how often words or short word sequences occur in a corpus. A single word is a unigram, a word pair is a bigram, and a word triple is a trigram; longer sequences follow the same naming pattern. Using these counts we can assign a probability to each candidate interpretation of a sentence and then pick the highest-probability one. The n-gram is the basic unit from which all of the models in this lecture are built: unigram, bigram, and trigram models
unit from which all of the models in this lecture are built: unigram, bigram, and trigram models differ only in how much preceding context they count.

An n-gram model is a probabilistic model that predicts the next word from the previous N minus one words. Such statistical models of word sequences are called language models. The order of the model is set by how many previous words it conditions on: a unigram model uses no context, a bigram model uses one previous word, and a trigram model uses the two previous words. This definition frames the rest of the lecture, which works through unigram, bigram, and trigram language
frames the rest of the lecture, which works through unigram, bigram, and trigram language models in turn.

The training data is a large set of sentences. We write the training set as D_train, a collection of M sentences x^1 through x^M. Each sentence x is an ordered list of N words, x = [x_1, ..., x_N]. A concrete example is x = [<s>, The, water, is, clear, ., </s>]. The special symbol <s> denotes the start of the sentence and </s> denotes the end of the sentence. These sentence boundary markers matter: they let the model condition on the fact that a word begins or ends a
boundary markers matter: they let the model condition on the fact that a word begins or ends a sentence, which is important once we move to bigram and higher order models.

We obtain the statistics for a language model from a corpus, a representative collection of documents. The British National Corpus (BNC) contains about 100 million words spread across roughly 4,000 documents, including newspaper articles, academic papers, school essays, memos, and radio phone-ins. At a far larger scale, the Google n-gram web corpus contains over one trillion words, precisely 1,024,908,267,229. The size and variety of the corpus directly affect the quality of

precisely 1,024,908,267,229. The size and variety of the corpus directly affect the quality of the resulting model: broader coverage means fewer unseen words and more reliable counts, which is why very large corpora are attractive for n-gram estimation.

The goal of a language model is to return the probability of an unseen sentence x, written P(x) = P(x_1, ..., x_n), for every sentence drawn from the vocabulary V. Here V is the vocabulary and the space of all possible sentences is V raised to the maximum sentence length, an astronomically large set. Because we can never enumerate or directly count every possible sentence, we need a way to compute this probability from more basic quantities. The different language models in
a way to compute this probability from more basic quantities. The different language models in this lecture are simply different answers to the question of how to decompose and estimate P(x).

The unigram language model computes the probability of a sentence by multiplying together the probability of each word appearing, estimated over the entire corpus. Formally P(x) is the product over positions n of P(x_n), and each P(x_n) is the count of that word divided by the total number of word tokens in the corpus. This assumes every word is independent of the others. As a worked example over a tiny three-sentence corpus, the probability of the two-word sequence 'i love'

example over a tiny three-sentence corpus, the probability of the two-word sequence 'i love' is P(i) times P(love), which equals 2/20 times 1/20, giving 0.005. The unigram model is the simplest possible language model because it ignores context entirely.

Because the unigram model treats words independently and simply favours frequent tokens, it produces degenerate results. In the small example corpus the most probable single word is the start symbol <s>, which occurs 3 times out of 20 tokens. It follows that the most probable single-word sentence is just '<s>', the most probable two-word sentence is '<s> <s>', and in general the most probable N-word sentence is the start symbol repeated N times. This is clearly nonsense as

most probable N-word sentence is the start symbol repeated N times. This is clearly nonsense as language and shows that a model with no notion of context cannot capture how words actually follow one another.

Rather than assuming independence, maximum likelihood estimation lets each word depend on all the words before it. By the chain rule of probability, the joint probability of a sentence factorises exactly: P(x) = P(x_1) times P(x_2 | x_1) times P(x_3 | x_1, x_2) and so on, up to P(x_N | x_1, ..., x_{N-1}). Written compactly, P(x) is the product over n of P(x_n | x_1, ..., x_{n-1}). This decomposition is exact and makes no approximation, so it captures the full dependency of

metadata.section_title: Maximum likelihood estimation and the chain rule

page_content: This decomposition is exact and makes no approximation, so it captures the full dependency of each word on everything that precedes it. The difficulty is purely in estimating those long conditional probabilities from data.

metadata.section_title: Maximum likelihood estimation and the chain rule

page_content: Estimating the full chain-rule conditionals directly runs into a sparsity problem. Each conditional P(x_n | x_{n-1} ... x_1) is estimated as the count of the whole sequence x_1 ... x_n divided by the count of the prefix x_1 ... x_{n-1}. As we condition on more and more preceding words, these longer sequences appear fewer and fewer times in any finite corpus, so the counts become sparser and many are zero. A zero count makes the estimated probability zero or undefined, so we

sparser and many are zero. A zero count makes the estimated probability zero or undefined, so we cannot reliably estimate probabilities that condition on long histories. This motivates the Markov approximation used by n-gram models.

A bigram language model assumes that the choice of a word depends only on the one word before it. The sentence probability becomes the product over positions n of P(x_n | x_{n-1}), and each bigram probability is estimated as the count of the pair (x_{n-1}, x_n) divided by the count of the preceding word x_{n-1}. This is an instance of the k-th order Markov assumption, which approximates the full history P(x_n | x_{n-1}, ..., x_1) by a fixed window P(x_n | x_{n-1}, ...,

metadata.section_title: Bigram language models and the Markov assumption

page_content: approximates the full history P(x_n | x_{n-1}, ..., x_1) by a fixed window P(x_n | x_{n-1}, ..., x_{n-k}). The bigram model is the special case with k equal to 1. The Markov assumption, named after Andrey Markov, is what makes n-gram estimation tractable by limiting how far back the model looks.

metadata.section_title: Bigram language models and the Markov assumption

page_content: To build a bigram model in practice we start from raw counts. A table of unigram counts gives how often each word occurs; for example arctic 100, monkeys 600, are 4000, my 3000, favourite 500, band 200. A bigram count matrix records how often each ordered word pair occurs, with rows indexed by the previous word x_{i-1} and columns by the current word x_i. To turn the count matrix into probabilities we divide each cell by the unigram count of its row word. For instance the

metadata.section_title: Bigram LM: from counts to probabilities

page_content: into probabilities we divide each cell by the unigram count of its row word. For instance the pair (arctic, monkeys) occurs 10 times and arctic occurs 100 times, so P(monkeys | arctic) is 10 divided by 100, which is 0.1. Doing this for every cell yields the full matrix of bigram probabilities.

metadata.section_title: Bigram LM: from counts to probabilities

page_content: Consider the sentence x = [arctic, monkeys, are, my, favourite, band]. Under a bigram model its probability is the product of the successive bigram probabilities: P(monkeys | arctic) times P(are | monkeys) times P(my | are) times P(favourite | my) times P(band | favourite). Each of these is a bigram count divided by the relevant unigram count. Plugging in the values 0.1, 0.417, 0.15, 0.1, and 0.1 gives a sentence probability of about 0.0000625. This tiny number is typical:

0.15, 0.1, and 0.1 gives a sentence probability of about 0.0000625. This tiny number is typical: because probabilities are multiplied, even a plausible sentence receives a very small absolute probability, which is why log probabilities are used in practice.

A second worked example uses three short sentences: '<s> a blue house </s>', '<s> a grey house </s>', and '<s> the grey house has the blue table </s>'. From these we can read off bigram probabilities such as P(a | <s>) = 2/3, P(the | <s>) = 1/3, P(</s> | house) = 2/3, and P(house | grey) = 2/2 = 1. We can also read off trigram probabilities, which condition on the two previous words: P(blue | <s> a) = 1/2 and P(house | a blue) = 1/1. The example shows how the same corpus

metadata.section_title: Bigram and trigram probabilities: the house example

page_content: words: P(blue | <s> a) = 1/2 and P(house | a blue) = 1/1. The example shows how the same corpus supports estimates at different n-gram orders simply by counting longer or shorter contexts.

metadata.section_title: Bigram and trigram probabilities: the house example

page_content: A general n-gram model conditions on some context, with P(x | context) = c(context, x) / c(context). In a bigram model the context is the single previous word x_{n-1}; in a trigram model it is the two previous words x_{n-2}, x_{n-1}; and so on. Longer contexts have a genuine advantage: they are more likely to capture long-range dependencies. In 'I saw a tiger that was really very ...', a long enough context helps decide that the next word is 'fierce' rather than 'talkative'.

...', a long enough context helps decide that the next word is 'fierce' rather than 'talkative'. But there is a trade-off, because longer contexts also make the counts sparser and produce more zero probabilities. In practice five-grams together with training sets of billions of tokens are common, balancing context length against data sparsity.

N-gram models can generate text by sampling words according to their probabilities, and the fluency of the output improves sharply with the order of the model. Sampling from unigram probabilities over a corpus of airline reservation queries yields word salad such as 'Of aircraft fare east', because words are chosen with no regard for their neighbours. A bigram model produces locally coherent fragments like 'I want a first class' and 'I would like to San Francisco'. A trigram

coherent fragments like 'I want a first class' and 'I would like to San Francisco'. A trigram model does better still, generating near-grammatical sentences such as 'How much does it cost' and "I'd like to depart before five o'clock pm". The progression from unigram to bigram to trigram shows how more context yields more natural sentences, even though none of these simple models is fully grammatical.

The Google Books n-gram viewer is a public tool, available at books.google.com/ngrams, that plots how often a word or short phrase appears in a large corpus of digitised books over time. Entering a phrase such as 'I scream' with a wildcard shows the changing relative frequency of its various continuations, like 'I scream at' or 'I scream and', across two centuries. It is a concrete illustration of n-gram statistics at very large scale and a convenient way to see how word
illustration of n-gram statistics at very large scale and a convenient way to see how word usage shifts historically.

If a word was never encountered during training, any sentence containing it receives a probability of zero. This is unavoidable in practice because all corpora are finite and new words are constantly emerging. A common solution is to introduce a special UNKNOWN token, usually written UNK, that stands in for every word not in the vocabulary, so out-of-vocabulary words are mapped to it rather than breaking the model. A refinement is to use several classes of unknown word, for

it rather than breaking the model. A refinement is to use several classes of unknown word, for example separate placeholders for names and for numbers, which retains a little information about what kind of token was unseen.

To train and evaluate a language model responsibly we split the data into three parts: a training set for estimating the model, a development (dev) set for tuning hyperparameters, and a test set for final evaluation on data the model has never seen. Evaluation itself comes in two broad flavours. Intrinsic evaluation measures the model directly, for example by accuracy or perplexity on held-out text. Extrinsic evaluation measures the model indirectly through its effect on a

metadata.section_title: Evaluating language models: train, dev and test

page_content: on held-out text. Extrinsic evaluation measures the model indirectly through its effect on a downstream task such as speech recognition or machine translation. Keeping the test set strictly separate is essential for an honest estimate of performance.

metadata.section_title: Evaluating language models: train, dev and test

page_content: Accuracy is an intrinsic measure that asks how well the language model predicts the next word. Given a prefix such as 'I always order pizza with cheese and ...', the model proposes a continuation, and we check whether it matches the word that actually followed. Candidate continuations like 'mushrooms', 'bread', or 'and' are scored against the truth. Accuracy is simply how often the model predicts the correct next word, and higher accuracy is better. It is easy to interpret

the model predicts the correct next word, and higher accuracy is better. It is easy to interpret but coarse, because it only rewards the single top prediction and ignores how much probability mass the model placed on the correct word.

Perplexity is an intrinsic measure of a model's ability to predict the words of an unseen text, meaning text that was not in the training data, such as the test set. It is computed as the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood of the test set, normalised by the total number of words N. Concretely, one sums the log probability the model assigns to each test word, negates and averages it over all words, and exponentiates the result. Lower perplexity indicates a

and averages it over all words, and exponentiates the result. Lower perplexity indicates a better model, because a lower value means the model was, on average, less surprised by the held-out words it had to predict.

Extrinsic evaluation judges a language model by how much it helps a real downstream application rather than by any intrinsic score. Typical tasks include sentence completion, grammatical error correction, where the model detects odd sentences and proposes alternatives, and natural language generation, where it is used to prefer more natural sounding sentences. It is also evaluated within speech recognition and machine translation systems. The advantage of extrinsic evaluation

within speech recognition and machine translation systems. The advantage of extrinsic evaluation is that it measures what ultimately matters, namely whether the model improves the end task, though it is more expensive to run than an intrinsic score like perplexity.

A serious problem arises when words that are in our vocabulary appear together in a context that was never seen in the training data. Under plain maximum likelihood estimation such unseen combinations are assigned zero probability, which then drives the probability of any sentence containing them to zero. Smoothing, also called discounting, is the family of techniques that fixes this. The guiding intuition is memorably summarised as stealing from the rich and giving to the

this. The guiding intuition is memorably summarised as stealing from the rich and giving to the poor: we take a little probability mass away from frequently seen events and redistribute it to unseen ones so that nothing has exactly zero probability.

The intuition behind smoothing is that we often want to make estimates from sparse statistics. Suppose after 'denied the' we saw 3 allegations, 2 reports, 1 claims and 1 request, seven observations in total, and zero of many other plausible words like charges, motion or benefits. A raw estimate gives all those unseen words zero probability. Smoothing flattens this spiky distribution so it generalises better, for example shaving the counts to 2.5 allegations, 1.5 reports, 0.5

so it generalises better, for example shaving the counts to 2.5 allegations, 1.5 reports, 0.5 claims and 0.5 request while reserving 2 units of probability mass for the 'other' unseen words. In short, smoothing takes from the frequent and gives to the rare, which is exactly what discounting means.

Add-1 smoothing, also known as Laplace smoothing, adds one to every count. The smoothed unigram probability of a word becomes its count plus one, divided by the corpus size plus the vocabulary size |V|. The effect is to pretend that we have seen every word in the vocabulary at least once, so no word is left with zero probability. It is the simplest smoothing method and is easy to apply, but adding a full count to every possible event is a blunt instrument that can move too
apply, but adding a full count to every possible event is a blunt instrument that can move too much probability mass onto events that were never actually observed.

Add-k smoothing generalises add-1 by adding a fractional constant k rather than a whole one, with k chosen to be less than one. The smoothed probability of a word is its count plus k, divided by the corpus size plus k times the vocabulary size |V|. The motivation is that add-1 puts too much probability mass on unseen words, so a smaller k is usually better. Here k is a hyperparameter: rather than fixing it in advance, we choose its optimal value on the development set, tuning
rather than fixing it in advance, we choose its optimal value on the development set, tuning it to whatever value gives the best held-out performance.

Interpolation is motivated by a tension between how informative a context is and how often it occurs. Longer contexts are more informative: knowing the previous word, as in 'dog bites ...', is more useful than knowing nothing, as in 'bites ...'. But a longer context only helps if it is frequent enough to have reliable counts; a rare context such as 'canid bites ...' may be too sparse to trust over the shorter 'bites ...'. This raises the question of whether we can combine

sparse to trust over the shorter 'bites ...'. This raises the question of whether we can combine evidence from unigram, bigram and trigram probabilities to get the best of both, which is exactly what interpolation does.

Simple linear interpolation combines the different n-gram estimates as a weighted average. For a trigram model the interpolated probability of x_n given the two previous words is lambda_3 times the trigram probability, plus lambda_2 times the bigram probability, plus lambda_1 times the unigram probability. The weights lambda_i must all be positive and sum to one, which guarantees the result is a valid probability. In effect the model hedges between orders, leaning on the

the result is a valid probability. In effect the model hedges between orders, leaning on the higher-order estimate when it is reliable and falling back on lower orders otherwise. The values of the lambdas are not guessed but chosen by parameter tuning on the development set.

Backoff takes a different approach from interpolation. It starts with an n-gram order of k, and only if the relevant count is zero does it back off to the shorter order k minus one, recursively, until it finds a context it has seen. In its naive form, simply using the lower-order probability whenever a count is zero does not yield a proper probability distribution, because the reserved mass is not accounted for. Proper backoff therefore uses a discounted higher-order

the reserved mass is not accounted for. Proper backoff therefore uses a discounted higher-order probability when the count is positive and, otherwise, multiplies the backed-off lower-order probability by a backoff weight alpha. The backoff weight is computed so that the distribution is respected, staying between zero and one and summing to one, as described in Jurafsky and Martin.

For further reading on language modelling, the recommended sources are Chapter 3 of Jurafsky and Martin, Chapter 6 of Eisenstein, and Michael Collins' lecture notes on language models. These cover n-gram models, maximum likelihood estimation, smoothing, interpolation and backoff in more depth than the lecture, and are the primary references for the material in this week.

The lecture traces the evolution of language models through four major stages: n-gram models, word2vec embeddings, recurrent neural networks, and the Transformer, with an open question mark for whatever comes next. Each stage addresses limitations of the one before it. N-gram models estimate the probability of a word from a short fixed window of preceding words. Word2vec replaces sparse symbolic representations with dense learned vectors. Recurrent neural networks introduce a

symbolic representations with dense learned vectors. Recurrent neural networks introduce a hidden state that can, in principle, carry information across an entire sequence. Transformers discard recurrence in favour of attention, enabling parallel training and strong long-range modelling. This progression frames the rest of the lecture, which examines word2vec, RNNs, and Transformers in turn.

A traditional way to represent word meaning is to use symbolic lexical resources such as WordNet. In this approach meaning is captured through explicit, manually defined relations between words. Two central relations are synonymy, which links words with the same meaning, and hypernymy, the is-a relation that connects a word to a more general category, for example dog to animal. WordNet organises nouns, verbs and other parts of speech into synsets and records relations such as

metadata.section_title: Representing Word Meaning with Symbolic Resources

page_content: organises nouns, verbs and other parts of speech into synsets and records relations such as hyponyms, meronyms and holonyms. Meaning here is discrete, human-curated and relational rather than statistical.

metadata.section_title: Representing Word Meaning with Symbolic Resources

page_content: Symbolic lexical resources like WordNet have several important limitations. They are static and incomplete, so they cannot keep pace with new words, new senses, or shifts in usage. They are expensive to maintain because they rely on expert human annotation. Crucially, they offer only a limited notion of similarity: relations are present or absent, with no natural way to express graded similarity between words, and they cannot capture the subtle, usage-based differences in
graded similarity between words, and they cannot capture the subtle, usage-based differences in meaning that emerge from how words are actually used in text.

A simple way to represent words numerically is the discrete or one-hot encoding, in which each word is treated as an atomic symbol. Every word becomes a vector that is zero everywhere except for a single position set to one. For example, motel and hotel each activate a different index in a long vector whose length equals the vocabulary size, so the vocabulary size becomes the dimensionality of the representation and can be very large. The key limitation is that all words are

of the representation and can be very large. The key limitation is that all words are equally dissimilar: because any two one-hot vectors are orthogonal, the cosine similarity between motel and hotel is zero even though the words are closely related. One-hot vectors therefore encode identity but carry no information about meaning or similarity.

Distributional semantics is captured by Firth's slogan that you shall know a word by the company it keeps. The core idea is that a word's meaning can be inferred from the contexts in which it appears. The word bank illustrates this: in one context it is a financial institution that accepts deposits, while in another it refers to the land alongside a body of water. The same surface form takes on different meanings depending on the surrounding words. Under this view, meaning

form takes on different meanings depending on the surrounding words. Under this view, meaning becomes statistical rather than symbolic, grounded in patterns of co-occurrence observed across large amounts of text.

Context-based representations turn the distributional idea into numbers by building a word-context co-occurrence matrix. Each target word is described by the words that surround it. In this matrix the rows are target words, the columns are context words, and the values are frequency counts of how often each context word appears near each target word within a chosen window. Words that occur in similar contexts end up with similar rows, so the geometry of the matrix begins to
that occur in similar contexts end up with similar rows, so the geometry of the matrix begins to reflect meaning. This count-based representation is the direct ancestor of learned word embeddings.

Raw co-occurrence count matrices have practical problems that make them awkward to use directly. They are extremely high-dimensional, because both rows and columns scale with the vocabulary. They are sparse and memory-intensive, since most word pairs never co-occur, leaving the matrix dominated by zeros. They are also sensitive to corpus size and to raw frequency effects, so very common words can dominate the counts. These issues motivate compressing the counts into a
very common words can dominate the counts. These issues motivate compressing the counts into a lower-dimensional, dense representation.

Instead of a huge sparse count matrix, we can represent each word as a dense vector of fixed dimensionality, typically between 100 and 300 dimensions for word2vec, learned automatically from data. These low-dimensional dense embeddings place similar words near one another in a continuous space. The core idea of word2vec is to learn such embeddings through a prediction task rather than by tabulating explicit co-occurrence counts: the model learns word vectors by predicting

than by tabulating explicit co-occurrence counts: the model learns word vectors by predicting context. Replacing counting with prediction yields compact vectors that generalise well and support graded similarity between words.

Word2vec comes in two training architectures that share the same underlying goal of learning useful word vectors. Continuous Bag-of-Words, or CBOW, predicts a target word from its surrounding context words. Skip-gram does the reverse, predicting the surrounding context words from a single target word. Both objectives push words that share contexts toward similar vectors, but they differ in which side of the context-target relationship serves as input and which serves as the
differ in which side of the context-target relationship serves as input and which serves as the prediction. The two variants have different strengths depending on word frequency and corpus size.

In the Continuous Bag-of-Words model the input is the set of surrounding context words and the output is the target word. The context word vectors are summed or averaged into a single representation, which is then used to predict the missing centre word. Because the context is pooled, CBOW is efficient and tends to work well for frequent words. Intuitively, CBOW answers the question: given the context, what word fits here? For the sentence eat an apple every day, CBOW would
given the context, what word fits here? For the sentence eat an apple every day, CBOW would try to predict apple from the words eat, an, every and day.

In the Skip-gram model the input is a single target word and the output is its surrounding context words. From one centre word the model generates several training pairs, one per context position, which gives it more learning signal per occurrence. Skip-gram often performs better than CBOW for rare words because each rare word directly participates in many predictions. Intuitively, Skip-gram answers the question: given this word, what words tend to appear nearby? For eat an
Skip-gram answers the question: given this word, what words tend to appear nearby? For eat an apple every day, Skip-gram would predict eat, an, every and day from the word apple.

CBOW and Skip-gram are mirror images of each other. CBOW predicts the target word apple from the context set eat, an, every, day, pooling the context into one prediction. Skip-gram instead predicts the context words eat, an, every, day from the single target word apple, producing multiple training pairs from each centre word. CBOW is faster and stronger on frequent words, whereas Skip-gram gives better representations for rare words at the cost of generating more training
Skip-gram gives better representations for rare words at the cost of generating more training examples. Choosing between them is a trade-off between speed and quality on infrequent vocabulary.

The CBOW training objective maximises the probability of each word given its context across the corpus. Formally the model maximises the product over all words w in the corpus of P(w given context of w). Because products of many probabilities are numerically awkward, we take the logarithm and instead maximise the sum over all words of log P(w given context of w). This log-likelihood objective is what gradient-based training optimises, adjusting the word and context vectors so
objective is what gradient-based training optimises, adjusting the word and context vectors so that observed word-context pairs receive high probability.

Learned word embeddings are useful as input features for a wide range of downstream natural language processing tasks. Examples include dependency parsing, named entity recognition, document classification, sentiment analysis, paraphrase detection, word clustering and machine translation. In each case the dense vectors provide a similarity-aware representation of words that a task-specific model can build on, which usually works better than starting from sparse one-hot
a task-specific model can build on, which usually works better than starting from sparse one-hot inputs.

Word embeddings exhibit linear regularities that can be tested through word analogies. Semantic and syntactic relationships are captured as consistent vector offsets, so an analogy of the form a is to b as c is to d can be solved with vector arithmetic. The classic example is man is to woman as king is to queen: taking the vector for king, subtracting man and adding woman lands near the vector for queen. Formally the answer is the word whose vector maximises the cosine

near the vector for queen. Formally the answer is the word whose vector maximises the cosine similarity with the vector w_b minus w_a plus w_c. This empirical property was highlighted by Mikolov and colleagues around 2013 to 2014.

Word embedding spaces trained on different languages tend to have similar geometric structure, so related concepts occupy analogous positions across languages. For instance, the vectors for the numbers one through five in English and their Spanish counterparts uno through cinco form similar shapes. This geometric alignment enables bilingual lexicon induction, where a mapping between the two spaces reveals word translations, and it is a precursor to modern multilingual
between the two spaces reveals word translations, and it is a precursor to modern multilingual embeddings that place many languages in a shared space.

A recurrent neural network is a network that contains a cycle: the hidden state produced at one time step is fed back and used at the next time step. Diagrams often show an RNN as a compact loop that can be unrolled across time into a chain of repeated cells, each passing a hidden state to its successor. This recurrence lets the network build up a representation of a sequence as it reads through it, one element at a time, rather than treating each input independently.

In a simple RNN, sometimes called an Elman network, the sequence is processed one token at a time from left to right. At each time step t the hidden state is updated from two inputs: the current input x_t and the hidden state from the previous time step h_{t-1}. The hidden layer therefore has a recurrent connection, so its value at time t depends on the whole history seen so far, summarised in h_{t-1}. The resulting hidden state h_t acts as a summary of past inputs and is

summarised in h_{t-1}. The resulting hidden state h_t acts as a summary of past inputs and is used to compute the output at time t. Weight matrices U and W combine the previous hidden state and the current input, and a matrix V maps the hidden state to the output.

An RNN language model processes an input sequence one word at a time and predicts the next word from the current word and the previous hidden state. At each step it produces a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token, so the hidden state carries the context needed to make that prediction. Because each step depends on the previous hidden state, the computation is inherently sequential, which limits how much it can be parallelised across time steps.

Inside an RNN language model, let t be the current time step and w_t the current word. The embedding e_t is the vector for the current word w_t. The hidden state h_t is a combination of the current embedding e_t and the previous hidden state h_{t-1}, so it accumulates information from all earlier words. Multiplying the hidden state by the output matrix, written V h, produces a vector of scores over the whole vocabulary. Passing these scores through a softmax yields y_t, a

vector of scores over the whole vocabulary. Passing these scores through a softmax yields y_t, a probability distribution over the vocabulary, and the entry y_t[i] is the probability that a particular word i is the next word.

An RNN language model is trained on a corpus so that at each time step it learns to predict the correct next word, minimising the error in that prediction. The loss is the difference between the predicted probability distribution and the correct distribution, measured by cross-entropy. The correct distribution is a one-hot vector over the vocabulary in which the actual next word has probability one and every other word has probability zero. During training the model is given

probability one and every other word has probability zero. During training the model is given the correct history rather than its own previous predictions, a technique called teacher forcing. Gradient descent then adjusts the weights to minimise the cross-entropy loss averaged over the sequence.

RNN language models can generate text by autoregressive generation, in which the word produced at each time step is conditioned on the word selected at the previous step. Generation typically starts from a sentence-start symbol, samples a word from the softmax distribution, feeds that sampled word back in as the next input, and continues until an end-of-sentence symbol is produced or a length limit is reached. The same autoregressive scheme underlies many applications beyond

or a length limit is reached. The same autoregressive scheme underlies many applications beyond plain next-word prediction, such as machine translation and summarisation, where a richer context replaces the simple start symbol as the initial condition.

The key difference between n-gram and RNN language models lies in how much context each can use. An n-gram language model incorporates information only from a limited, fixed context, namely the preceding n minus one tokens. An RNN language model, by contrast, maintains a hidden state that can in principle incorporate information from all of the preceding words in the sequence. This gives RNNs a longer effective memory than fixed-order n-gram models.

Despite their longer memory, RNNs have significant limitations. They process input sequentially, which makes both training and inference slow. Even with LSTM and GRU improvements they struggle to capture long-range dependencies. Their sequential nature limits parallelisation during training, making them hard to scale to very large datasets. They are prone to vanishing and exploding gradients over long sequences, and they find it difficult to capture global context
exploding gradients over long sequences, and they find it difficult to capture global context effectively. These weaknesses motivated a different architecture, the Transformer.

The Transformer, proposed by Vaswani and colleagues in 2017 in the paper Attention is All You Need, marked a turning point for language models. It eliminates recurrence, so there is no step-by-step token processing, and this enables parallelisation: entire sequences are processed simultaneously, which makes training much faster. The Transformer leverages self-attention to model long-range dependencies directly, and it achieved state-of-the-art results in machine translation
dependencies directly, and it achieved state-of-the-art results in machine translation and well beyond.

Transformers are used in three broad configurations. Encoder-only models are suited to natural language understanding tasks such as classification and feature extraction; examples include BERT, RoBERTa and DeBERTa. Encoder-decoder models handle sequence-to-sequence mapping such as translation and summarisation; examples include T5, Flan-T5 and BART. Decoder-only models are used for natural language generation, translation, summarisation and text completion; examples include

natural language generation, translation, summarisation and text completion; examples include the GPT family and LLaMA, which describe most recent large language models. The choice of family reflects whether the task is primarily understanding, generation, or mapping one sequence to another.

At a high level a Transformer maps an input sequence to an output sequence, for example translating je suis etudiant into I am a student. It is built from a stack of encoders and a stack of decoders. The encoder stack produces contextual representations of the input, and the decoder stack uses the encoder's output together with the decoder's own previous outputs to generate the target sequence. Each encoder passes its output up to the next encoder, and the top encoder's

target sequence. Each encoder passes its output up to the next encoder, and the top encoder's representations are made available to every decoder. The bottom of the encoder stack receives word embeddings as input. The guiding principle is that there is no recurrence and no convolution, only attention.

Self-attention replaced recurrence for two main reasons. In RNNs, information between distant tokens must flow through a number of steps that grows with the distance, on the order of n steps, and the computation is sequential and therefore hard to parallelise. In Transformers, self-attention lets every token attend directly to every other token in the sequence in a single layer, producing contextualised representations, and the computation within each layer can be

layer, producing contextualised representations, and the computation within each layer can be parallelised across sequence positions. The trade-off is cost: attention time and memory scale quadratically with the sequence length, on the order of n squared.

An encoder layer refines token representations through a fixed sequence of operations. First, self-attention mixes information across positions so that each token can incorporate context from the others. The result is combined with the layer's input through a residual connection and passed through layer normalisation. Next, a position-wise feed-forward network applies a nonlinear transformation independently to each token. This is again wrapped in a residual connection and

transformation independently to each token. This is again wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalisation, so each sub-layer computes LayerNorm of x plus SelfAttention of x, and then LayerNorm of z plus FFN of z. Within a layer the tokens are processed in parallel yet coupled through attention, deeper layers progressively refine the contextual representations, and the residual connections preserve signal and ease optimisation.

Self-attention is implemented as scaled dot-product attention. For an input X, three matrices are formed by learned linear projections: queries Q equal X times W_Q, keys K equal X times W_K, and values V equal X times W_V. The attention output is softmax of Q times K transpose divided by the square root of d_k, all times V. The dot products Q K transpose measure similarity between queries and keys in the projected space. Dividing by the square root of the key dimension d_k

queries and keys in the projected space. Dividing by the square root of the key dimension d_k prevents the dot products from growing too large in high dimensions, which keeps gradients stable. The softmax converts these scores into a distribution over the input elements, and the output is a weighted sum of the value vectors.

Self-attention is often explained through an information-retrieval analogy with three roles. The query Q represents the current element and what it is looking for, for example looking for action movies with strong female leads. The key K represents the features of each element against which the query is compared, for example a movie tagged as action, drama and female lead; every input element has an associated key. The value V holds the actual content that may be returned if

element has an associated key. The value V holds the actual content that may be returned if the key matches the query, for example the full movie details. Attention compares the query against all keys to decide how much of each value to include in the output.

Self-attention can be computed in four steps. Step one: for each token compute a query, a key and a value vector by multiplying its embedding with the learned weight matrices W_Q, W_K and W_V. Step two: compute attention scores as dot products between a token's query and every key, giving one score per token pair, where a larger dot product means stronger alignment. Step three: scale each score by dividing by the square root of the key dimension, for example the square root

each score by dividing by the square root of the key dimension, for example the square root of 64 which is 8, to prevent large magnitudes and stabilise gradients, then apply softmax so the weights are positive and form a probability distribution over tokens. Step four: multiply each value vector by its attention weight and sum them, which emphasises important tokens and down-weights irrelevant ones, producing the updated contextualised representation that is passed to the

irrelevant ones, producing the updated contextualised representation that is passed to the feed-forward layer. A worked example scores q1 dot k1 equal to 112 and q1 dot k2 equal to 96, which after scaling become 14 and 12 and after softmax become 0.88 and 0.12.

In practice self-attention is computed for the whole sequence at once using matrices. The token embeddings are packed into a matrix X, and multiplying X by the weight matrices W_Q, W_K and W_V yields the query, key and value matrices Q, K and V for the entire context in one operation. The output of the self-attention layer is then Z equal to softmax of Q times K transpose divided by the square root of d_k, all times V. This matrix form is mathematically equivalent to

divided by the square root of d_k, all times V. This matrix form is mathematically equivalent to computing attention token by token but is far more efficient on modern hardware because it is fully parallelised.

Rather than computing a single attention function, each self-attention layer runs several attention heads in parallel, an idea called multi-head attention. Instead of one set of query, key and value weight matrices, the model uses multiple sets, one per head, each producing its own output matrix such as Z0 through Z7 for eight heads. The heads operate independently in different learned projection subspaces, so each can capture different aspects or relational patterns in the

projection subspaces, so each can capture different aspects or relational patterns in the same input, for example distinguishing the river sense of bank from the financial sense. The head outputs are concatenated and multiplied by a learnable output projection matrix W_O to produce the final output Z, which integrates the diverse attention patterns and is passed to the next layer.

Because self-attention treats its inputs as a set, a Transformer has no built-in notion of word order. To supply order information, a positional vector is added to each input embedding. In the original Transformer these were fixed sinusoidal positional encodings, that is sinusoidal functions of different frequencies, one pattern per position, added to the token embeddings before the first layer. This lets the model reason about the relative and absolute positions of tokens

To stabilise training in deep networks, each sub-layer of a Transformer is wrapped in a residual connection. In both the self-attention and feed-forward sub-layers, the input is added to the sub-layer's output, and the sum is then passed through a layer normalisation step. These residual connections improve gradient flow and make deep architectures easier to optimise, which is part of why very deep Transformer stacks can be trained successfully.

The decoder generates output one token at a time and must not peek at future tokens. Its self-attention is therefore masked so that each position can only attend to earlier tokens, not later ones. This prevents information leakage from future tokens during training, where the whole target is available at once. Masking is implemented by setting the attention scores for future positions to negative infinity before the softmax, so those positions receive zero weight. In effect
to negative infinity before the softmax, so those positions receive zero weight. In effect each token is generated based only on the tokens that precede it.

In addition to masked self-attention, each decoder layer contains a cross-attention, or encoder-decoder attention, sub-layer that lets the decoder attend to the encoder's outputs when generating each token. The top encoder layer produces contextualised representations of the input, which are used as the keys and values in cross-attention, while the queries come from the decoder. Feeding these encoder representations into the decoder's cross-attention helps the decoder focus

Feeding these encoder representations into the decoder's cross-attention helps the decoder focus on the relevant input positions during generation, linking the source sequence to the sequence being produced.

Turning decoder states into output tokens differs between training and inference. At training time the full target sequence is known, so teacher forcing feeds the correct previous tokens to compute next-token predictions. At inference time the output is generated autoregressively, one token at a time, with each predicted token fed back into the decoder. A final linear layer projects the decoder output to the size of the vocabulary, a softmax converts these logits into a

the decoder output to the size of the vocabulary, a softmax converts these logits into a probability distribution over the vocabulary, and a token is selected, for example by greedy decoding or by sampling.

Transformers are trained by minimising a cross-entropy loss that measures how far the predicted token probabilities are from the true target tokens; lower loss indicates better predictions. Gradients of this loss are computed by backpropagation and used to update the model parameters, often with the Adam optimiser. The models are trained on paired input-output sequences, for example source and target sentences for translation.

Its key components are self-attention, multi-head attention, the encoder-decoder structure and positional encoding. It works well because the path length between any two tokens is short, on the order of one step per layer, the computation is fully parallelisable across sequence positions, and

page_content: The original Transformer contains both an encoder stack and a decoder stack, and three families of model are derived from it by keeping different parts. Encoder-only models keep the encoder stack alone. They are used for natural language understanding, classification, and feature extraction, because they produce contextual representations of an input rather than generating new text. Typical examples are BERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa. Encoder-decoder models keep both stacks, with

text. Typical examples are BERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa. Encoder-decoder models keep both stacks, with cross-attention letting the decoder attend to the encoded input. They are used for natural language generation tasks that are fundamentally sequence-to-sequence mappings, such as translation and summarisation, where a source sequence is transformed into a target sequence. Typical examples are T5, Flan-T5, and BART. Decoder-only models keep the decoder stack alone, with masked

examples are T5, Flan-T5, and BART. Decoder-only models keep the decoder stack alone, with masked multi-head self-attention. They are used for natural language generation, and can also perform translation, summarisation, and completion by treating them as continuation problems. Typical examples are the GPT series, LLaMA, and effectively every other new model released today.

Modern large language models are built from Transformer decoder blocks. The defining property of these blocks is causal attention: when computing the representation at a given position, the attention mask prevents the model from attending to any token that comes later in the sequence, so a position has access only to itself and to positions to its left. This makes generation left-to-right - the model emits one token at a time, and each emitted token becomes part of the

left-to-right - the model emits one token at a time, and each emitted token becomes part of the visible history for the next step. The contrast is with BERT, which is an encoder and is bidirectional: every position can attend to every other position, both left and right. Because BERT sees the whole sequence at once, it cannot be trained by simply predicting the next token, since the answer would be visible in the input. It is instead trained with masked language modelling,

the answer would be visible in the input. It is instead trained with masked language modelling, where tokens are corrupted and reconstructed from surrounding context on both sides. Bidirectional attention and masked LM give strong representations for understanding tasks, but they do not naturally produce a left-to-right generator.

GPT stands for Generative Pretrained Transformer, and it names a series of models released by OpenAI. These are decoder transfer language models: the decoder stack is pretrained on text and then transferred to downstream tasks, and because they are decoders they can be used for generative tasks rather than only for classification. The original GPT, released in 2018, used twelve stacked blocks, each with masked multi-head self-attention, layer normalisation, and a feed-forward

Downstream tasks were handled by serialising the task input into a single token sequence with delimiters and then reading a task-specific linear head off the top of the transformer. Classification passed start, text, and extract tokens; entailment passed a premise and a hypothesis separated by a delimiter; similarity passed the two

entailment passed a premise and a hypothesis separated by a delimiter; similarity passed the two texts in both orders and combined the results; multiple choice ran the context against each candidate answer separately and compared the scores. The same pretrained body served all of these.

Its corpus was WebText, built from outbound links from Reddit, and amounted to roughly forty gigabytes of text. The headline result was qualitative as much as quantitative: GPT-2 was notably good at generation tasks. GPT-3 demonstrated in-context learning, in which the model performs a task specified entirely within its prompt. In the zero-shot setting the prompt contains only a task description and the input, for example an instruction to translate English to French followed by the word cheese. In the one-shot setting the prompt contains the task description, a single worked example such as sea otter mapping to loutre de mer, and then the input. In the few-shot setting several worked

In all three settings the model's weights are unchanged: no gradient update takes place, and the examples act purely as context that conditions the next-token distribution. This contrasts directly with traditional fine-tuning, where each labelled example is fed to the model and followed by a gradient update, so that the weights themselves

Two ideas underpin the design. The first is that autoregressive models are naturally generative: because the model is defined as a distribution over the next token given the history, generating is just repeatedly sampling from that distribution, and the model can produce long stretches of coherent text. Autoregressive models also support in-context learning, since anything placed in the history conditions what comes next. The second idea is that the training is

anything placed in the history conditions what comes next. The second idea is that the training is self-supervised. No manual labels are needed and no annotators are employed. The training signal comes from the text itself, through the task of next-token prediction: every position in every document supplies its own target, namely the token that actually followed. Because the labels are manufactured from the raw data, the approach scales easily to massive datasets - the only
