A dictionary definition frames evaluation as an assessment of value, and in a computational setting that assessment is made concrete through numbers, scores, and

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: value, and in a computational setting that assessment is made concrete through numbers, scores, and repeatable tests. Treating evaluation as testing keeps the focus on measurable evidence: we run a system on data, compare its output against a known standard, and summarise the result with a metric that other people can reproduce.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: We evaluate NLP systems because evaluation tells us how well a system is actually performing rather than how well we assume it performs. Different stakeholders care for different reasons. Users care about whether a system is useful for a concrete task, while developers care about whether the system is improving from one version to the next. Beyond these day-to-day concerns, evaluation underpins several core activities in research and engineering: it enables fair comparison

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: evaluation underpins several core activities in research and engineering: it enables fair comparison between competing systems, supports debugging by localising where errors occur, guides model selection when several candidates exist, and provides the evidence needed for credible scientific reporting. Without evaluation, claims about progress cannot be trusted.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Performance evaluation in NLP is frequently based on a benchmark dataset, often organised around a community challenge or shared task such as SemEval or a Kaggle competition. In such a setup a specific task is defined precisely, and gold-standard data is provided, usually split into training, development, and test portions. The organisers also supply an automated means of scoring submissions. Scoring compares two things: the response, which is the system-generated set of

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: scoring submissions. Scoring compares two things: the response, which is the system-generated set of annotations or predictions, and the reference, which is the gold standard produced by humans. Because every participant is measured against the same reference under the same fixed protocol, benchmark datasets make results comparable across teams and over time.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Gold-standard data is the human-produced reference against which systems are judged, and it is time-consuming and costly to produce. Creating it requires clear annotation instructions, known as annotation guidelines, so that different people label the data in the same way. Annotation is typically carried out by experts, who may need some training in linguistics for harder tasks. To check quality, multiple annotators label the same subset of samples, and the consistency of

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: tasks. To check quality, multiple annotators label the same subset of samples, and the consistency of their labels is quantified through inter-annotator agreement. Reliable evaluation depends on reliable annotation: if the reference labels are noisy or inconsistent, every downstream score computed against them becomes untrustworthy. Some disagreement between annotators is normal and expected.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Human annotations are not always identical, because different annotators may interpret the same guideline differently. Inter-annotator agreement measures how consistently humans assign the same labels to the same data. It is used both to validate a dataset and to diagnose the task itself: high agreement suggests that the task definition and the annotation guidelines are clear and reliable, whereas low agreement is a warning that the guidelines are ambiguous or the task is

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: and reliable, whereas low agreement is a warning that the guidelines are ambiguous or the task is inherently hard. Agreement is therefore not just a property of the annotators but also evidence about the quality of the annotation scheme. The simplest measure is raw observed agreement, but it needs correcting for chance before it can be trusted.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Observed agreement, written P_a, is the proportion of items on which two annotators assign the same label. It is computed simply by dividing the number of items they agreed on by the total number of items. For example, if two annotators each label ten items and they give the same label on seven of them, the observed agreement is seven divided by ten, or 0.70. Observed agreement is intuitive and easy to compute, but it has an important weakness: it does not correct for

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: agreement is intuitive and easy to compute, but it has an important weakness: it does not correct for agreement that would occur purely by chance. Two annotators guessing randomly would still coincide on some items, so raw observed agreement tends to overstate the true reliability of the annotation.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Expected agreement, written P_e, estimates how much of the observed agreement could be explained by chance alone. It is derived from how often each annotator uses each label. Suppose annotator A labels six of ten items Positive and four Negative, while annotator B labels five Positive and five Negative. The chance of both independently choosing Positive is 0.6 times 0.5, which is 0.30, and the chance of both choosing Negative is 0.4 times 0.5, which is 0.20. Summing these

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: is 0.30, and the chance of both choosing Negative is 0.4 times 0.5, which is 0.20. Summing these gives an expected agreement of 0.50. This value is the baseline level of agreement we would expect even if the annotators were not truly coordinating, and it is the quantity that chance-corrected measures subtract away.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Cohen's Kappa corrects observed agreement for the agreement expected by chance. It is defined as the difference between observed and expected agreement divided by one minus expected agreement: K = (P_a - P_e) / (1 - P_e). The numerator measures how much the annotators agreed beyond chance, and the denominator measures how much room there was to exceed chance. Using the earlier figures, with observed agreement of 0.70 and expected agreement of 0.50, Kappa equals 0.20 divided

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: figures, with observed agreement of 0.70 and expected agreement of 0.50, Kappa equals 0.20 divided by 0.50, which is 0.40. Because it discounts chance agreement, Kappa is more informative than raw agreement alone, and it is the standard reliability statistic reported for categorical annotation tasks.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Consider two annotators labelling forty items as either yes or no. They both say yes on 31 items and both say no on 6 items; annotator 1 says yes while annotator 2 says no on 2 items, and the reverse happens on 1 item. Observed agreement is the sum of the cells where they agree, (31 + 6) divided by 40, which equals 0.925. Expected agreement is computed from the marginal totals: annotator 1 says yes 33 times and no 7 times, annotator 2 says yes 32 times and no 8 times, so P_e

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: annotator 1 says yes 33 times and no 7 times, annotator 2 says yes 32 times and no 8 times, so P_e is (33/40 times 32/40) plus (7/40 times 8/40), which equals 0.695. The resulting Kappa is (0.925 - 0.695) divided by (1 - 0.695), a high value indicating strong chance-corrected agreement.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: There is no single universal threshold for a good Kappa; several interpretation scales exist. Landis and Koch in 1977 proposed bands where values below 0.2 are slight, up to 0.4 fair, up to 0.6 moderate, up to 0.8 substantial, and above that almost perfect. Grove and colleagues in 1981, working in the psychiatric community, treated values above 0.6 as acceptable. Krippendorff in 1980 allowed tentative conclusions above 0.67 and definite conclusions above 0.8. Rietveld and van

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: 1980 allowed tentative conclusions above 0.67 and definite conclusions above 0.8. Rietveld and van Hout in 1993 used moderate from 0.4 to 0.6 and substantial from 0.6 to 0.8, while Green in 1997 called values below 0.4 low, from 0.4 to 0.75 fair to good, and above 0.75 high. The right scale depends on the field and the stakes of the task.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Evaluation of a two-class decision is organised with a confusion matrix built from four counts. A true positive is an item the system annotated that is actually correct; a false positive is an item the system annotated that should not have been; a false negative is a correct item the system failed to annotate; and a true negative is an item correctly left unannotated. A useful intuition is a picture of blue stars mixed with red circles, where the task is to select the blue

metadata.section_title: The Confusion Matrix: TP, FP, FN, TN
metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: intuition is a picture of blue stars mixed with red circles, where the task is to select the blue stars: stars correctly circled are true positives, circles wrongly included are false positives, a star left outside is a false negative, and circles correctly left out are true negatives. In one such illustration there are five true positives, two false positives, one false negative, and four true negatives. Most standard metrics are derived from these four counts.

metadata.section_title: The Confusion Matrix: TP, FP, FN, TN
metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Precision and recall summarise a confusion matrix from two complementary angles. Precision asks: of the items the system predicted as positive, how many were actually correct? It is true positives divided by the sum of true positives and false positives, TP / (TP + FP). Recall asks the opposite question: of the items that are truly positive, how many did the system manage to find? It is true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives, TP / (TP + FN). Using the

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: find? It is true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives, TP / (TP + FN). Using the blue-stars example with five true positives, two false positives and one false negative, precision is 5/7 which is about 0.714 and recall is 5/6 which is about 0.833. High precision means few false alarms; high recall means few misses; the two often trade off against each other.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: The F-score, also called the F-measure or F1-score, combines precision and recall into a single number using their harmonic mean rather than an ordinary average. The general form is the weighted harmonic mean F-beta = (beta squared + 1) times P times R divided by (beta squared times P plus R); setting beta to 1 gives the balanced F1 measure, F1 = 2PR / (P + R). The harmonic mean is deliberately conservative: it stays close to the smaller of the two values, so a system only

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: is deliberately conservative: it stays close to the smaller of the two values, so a system only earns a high F1 when both precision and recall are high together. This makes F1 especially useful when the positive class matters and the classes are imbalanced, because it refuses to reward a system that is strong on one measure but weak on the other.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: The reason F1 uses a harmonic mean becomes clear when it is compared with a plain arithmetic mean. When precision is 0.714 and recall is 0.833, the arithmetic mean is 0.774 and the F1 score is 0.769, so the two barely differ because the values are close. The gap widens dramatically when the values are far apart: with precision of 1.0 but recall of only 0.15, the arithmetic mean is a flattering 0.575, whereas F1 is just 0.261. The harmonic mean punishes the large imbalance and

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: a flattering 0.575, whereas F1 is just 0.261. The harmonic mean punishes the large imbalance and gives a truer picture of a system that finds almost nothing, which is exactly why F1 is preferred over a simple average when both precision and recall need to be respected at once.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Accuracy measures the proportion of all decisions that were correct, both positive and negative: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN). It is an appropriate summary when every class is roughly equally important and equally frequent. Its weakness appears on imbalanced data. If 95 percent of items belong to the negative class, a lazy system that always predicts negative achieves 95 percent accuracy while completely failing on the positive class, giving it a recall of zero. A concrete

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: accuracy while completely failing on the positive class, giving it a recall of zero. A concrete case is detecting hateful versus neutral text, where the harmful class is rare but is the one we care about most. In such situations accuracy is misleading and the F-score, which focuses on the positive class, is far more informative.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: When a task has several categories, their individual scores must be combined into an overall figure, and there are three common ways to do this. Macro-averaging computes the metric separately for each class and then averages those scores with equal weight, so every class counts the same regardless of size. Micro-averaging instead pools all true positives, false positives and false negatives across classes first and computes a single metric from the combined counts, which

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: false negatives across classes first and computes a single metric from the combined counts, which makes it dominated by frequent classes. For example, combining a Person class and a Location class, macro-averaging gives an F1 around 0.86 while micro-averaging gives about 0.82, because the two schemes weight the classes differently. Macro-averaging ignores class imbalance, micro-averaging is less sensitive to it, and a weighted average sits between them by weighting each class

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: micro-averaging is less sensitive to it, and a weighted average sits between them by weighting each class by its number of true instances.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Named entity recognition is scored at the level of whole entities rather than individual tokens, and a key rule is that a partially correct span does not count as a true positive. Consider the sentence 'Dr Maya Chen joined Acme Labs in Bristol.' The gold entities are Maya Chen as a person, Acme Labs as an organisation, and Bristol as a location. Suppose a system predicts Maya Chen as a person, only Acme as an organisation, and Bristol as a location. The person and location

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Chen as a person, only Acme as an organisation, and Bristol as a location. The person and location entities match exactly and count as true positives, but the organisation prediction is wrong on both sides: the incomplete span Acme is a false positive, and the full entity Acme Labs is a missed false negative. Requiring exact span boundaries makes entity-level evaluation stricter than token-level scoring.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Micro-averaged F1 for named entity recognition is obtained by pooling the per-type counts before computing any metric. Take an example with three entity types where the person type has one true positive, the organisation type has one false positive and one false negative, and the location type has one true positive. Pooling across all types gives a total of two true positives, one false positive, and one false negative. Micro precision is then 2 divided by (2 + 1) which is

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: one false positive, and one false negative. Micro precision is then 2 divided by (2 + 1) which is 0.667 and micro recall is likewise 2 divided by (2 + 1) which is 0.667, so the micro-averaged F1 is also 0.667. The interpretation is that micro-averaging produces one overall score after merging every entity decision across categories, treating each individual entity equally rather than each entity type equally.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Open Information Extraction, or OpenIE, extracts relational facts from text without relying on a fixed, predefined schema of relations. Its input is raw sentences or documents, and its output is a set of relation tuples, each usually taking the form of two arguments joined by a relation, written as (argument, relation, argument). This openness is what distinguishes it from traditional relation extraction, which can only fill in a closed list of relation types decided in

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: traditional relation extraction, which can only fill in a closed list of relation types decided in advance. By not committing to a schema, OpenIE can discover relations it was never explicitly told to look for, and its broader aim is to turn unstructured natural-language text into machine-readable knowledge that downstream systems can query and reason over.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: A concrete OpenIE example makes the tuple format clear. Given the sentence 'Albert Einstein published the theory of relativity in 1915,' a system might extract two tuples: (Albert Einstein; published; the theory of relativity) and (Albert Einstein; published in; 1915). Each tuple pairs entities with the relation that links them, capturing distinct facts drawn from the same sentence. Producing these tuples reliably depends heavily on earlier stages of the NLP pipeline, because

metadata.section_title: What an OpenIE Extraction Looks Like
metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: sentence. Producing these tuples reliably depends heavily on earlier stages of the NLP pipeline, because OpenIE builds on part-of-speech tagging to identify candidate arguments and relations, on parsing to recover grammatical structure, and on entity recognition to delimit the arguments. Errors made in those upstream steps propagate into the extracted facts.

metadata.section_title: What an OpenIE Extraction Looks Like
metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: Approaches to OpenIE have evolved over time. Classical methods relied on hand-built patterns, on the dependency structure of sentences, and on clause splitting to break complex sentences into simpler assertions. Later work moved toward supervised and neural approaches that learn to extract tuples from data. Regardless of method, several persistent challenges remain: lexical ambiguity, synonymy where different phrasings denote the same relation, coreference across sentences,

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: ambiguity, synonymy where different phrasings denote the same relation, coreference across sentences, and the trustworthiness or factual reliability of the extracted assertions. In the context of this lecture, OpenIE serves as a compact application case that shows how the earlier NLP components combine, rather than being the central focus of assessment.

metadata.lecture_title: Week 10 - Evaluation Methods and Open Information Extraction (final lecture)

page_content: The Transformer architecture underpins modern NLP models and can be organised into three families according to which parts of the original encoder-decoder design are kept. Encoder-only models retain just the encoder stack and are suited to natural language understanding, classification and feature extraction; representative examples include BERT, RoBERTa and DeBERTa. Encoder-decoder models keep both stacks and are used for natural language generation that maps one sequence to

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: Encoder-decoder models keep both stacks and are used for natural language generation that maps one sequence to another, such as translation, summarisation and other sequence-to-sequence problems; examples include T5, Flan-T5 and BART. Decoder-only models keep only the decoder and are used for generation, completion, translation and summarisation; examples include the GPT family and LLaMA, and most recent general-purpose models follow this design. BERT belongs to the

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: family and LLaMA, and most recent general-purpose models follow this design. BERT belongs to the encoder-only family, which is why it is a natural fit for understanding tasks rather than free-form generation.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: Before BERT, ELMo (Peters et al., 2018, winner of the NAACL 2018 best paper award) was an influential approach to contextual word representations. ELMo trains two separate unidirectional language models built on LSTMs: one that reads left to right and one that reads right to left. It follows a feature-based approach, meaning the pre-trained representations are supplied as fixed input features to separate task-specific models rather than fine-tuning the whole network end to

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: input features to separate task-specific models rather than fine-tuning the whole network end to end. ELMo was trained on single sentences drawn from the 1B Word Benchmark (Chelba et al., 2014). Its main drawbacks are that the two directions are only shallowly combined rather than jointly bidirectional, it is slow to adapt, it is a weaker backbone for downstream tasks, and it is hard to parallelise because of its recurrent LSTM structure.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a deep Transformer encoder pre-trained on large text corpora. Its central idea is to learn word representations from bidirectional context, using both the left and the right of a word at the same time. This matters because the surrounding words on both sides are needed to disambiguate meaning: in 'we went to the river bank' the word bank means a riverside, whereas in 'I need to go to bank to make a deposit' it

metadata.section_title: BERT key contributions and bidirectional context
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: river bank' the word bank means a riverside, whereas in 'I need to go to bank to make a deposit' it means a financial institution. BERT is pre-trained with two objectives used together: masked language modelling and next sentence prediction. On release in 2018 it achieved state-of-the-art results on a broad range of sentence-level and token-level tasks, which is what made bidirectional pre-training so influential.

metadata.section_title: BERT key contributions and bidirectional context
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: Masked language modelling (MLM) is BERT's main pre-training objective. Every input token participates in bidirectional self-attention, so each position can see the whole sequence, but only the roughly fifteen percent (15%) of tokens that are sampled for prediction contribute to the training loss. For those selected positions the model produces a softmax distribution over the entire vocabulary and is trained with cross-entropy loss; the objective is the average cross-entropy

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: entire vocabulary and is trained with cross-entropy loss; the objective is the average cross-entropy over the sampled positions. The network weights are updated based on this average loss over the sampled tokens. Because attention is bidirectional, the prediction of a masked word can draw on context from both sides at once, and this is precisely what makes the learned representations deeply bidirectional rather than left-to-right only.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: Masked language modelling can be illustrated with simple examples. Given the sentence 'He is from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia', BERT might mask two positions to produce 'He [MASK] from Kuala [MASK], Malaysia' and learn to recover the hidden words. Given 'He went to the store', a single token can be masked to give 'He went to the [MASK]'. During training the model reads the surrounding unmasked words and predicts a probability distribution over the vocabulary for each masked slot,

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: unmasked words and predicts a probability distribution over the vocabulary for each masked slot, so that the correct token should receive the highest probability. Only the masked, selected positions contribute to the prediction and therefore to the loss, while the remaining tokens serve purely as context.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT always masks a fixed fraction of tokens, with the rate k set to 15% (fifteen percent). The choice is a trade-off: masking too few tokens makes training computationally expensive because each sentence yields little learning signal, while masking too many tokens leaves too little surrounding context for the model to make good predictions. The tokens to mask are chosen by uniform random sampling across the sequence. Whether uniform sampling is optimal is an open question;

metadata.section_title: MLM masking rate and selection strategy
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: uniform random sampling across the sequence. Whether uniform sampling is optimal is an open question; later work such as span masking (Joshi et al., 2020, SpanBERT) masks contiguous spans of tokens instead of independent positions and can learn better representations for some tasks. A typical masked example produced this way is 'He [MASK] from Kuala [MASK], Malaysia'.

metadata.section_title: MLM masking rate and selection strategy
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: For the fifteen percent of tokens selected for prediction, BERT does not always replace them with the [MASK] symbol. Instead it applies an eighty-ten-ten corruption rule. Eighty percent of the time the chosen token is replaced with the special [MASK] token, so 'went to the store' becomes 'went to the [MASK]'. Ten percent of the time it is replaced with a random word from the vocabulary, so 'went to the store' becomes 'went to the running'. The remaining ten percent of the

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: vocabulary, so 'went to the store' becomes 'went to the running'. The remaining ten percent of the time the token is left unchanged, so 'went to the store' stays 'went to the store'. The reason for this mixture is that the [MASK] token never appears during fine-tuning, so relying on it exclusively would create a mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning; mixing in random and unchanged tokens forces the model to build good representations for every token rather than only

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: unchanged tokens forces the model to build good representations for every token rather than only for masked slots.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: Next sentence prediction (NSP) is BERT's second pre-training objective. Its motivation is that many downstream NLP tasks depend on understanding the relationship between two sentences, for example natural language inference, paraphrase detection and question answering. NSP is designed to narrow the gap between pre-training and fine-tuning by teaching the model about sentence pairs directly. Each training example is built from two segments. A [CLS] token is placed at the very

metadata.section_title: Next sentence prediction: motivation and format
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: directly. Each training example is built from two segments. A [CLS] token is placed at the very beginning of the input and a [SEP] token separates the two segments. When the second segment genuinely follows the first the label is IsNext; when the second segment is a random sentence the label is NotNext. For instance, pairing 'the man went to [MASK] store' with 'he bought a gallon [MASK] milk' is labelled IsNext, whereas pairing it with 'penguin [MASK] are flight ##less birds'

metadata.section_title: Next sentence prediction: motivation and format
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: [MASK] milk' is labelled IsNext, whereas pairing it with 'penguin [MASK] are flight ##less birds' is labelled NotNext.

metadata.section_title: Next sentence prediction: motivation and format
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: The next sentence prediction head reads the output vector associated with the [CLS] token, which acts as an aggregate representation of the whole pair. This [CLS] output is multiplied by a set of classification weights W_NSP and passed through a softmax, and the model is trained with cross-entropy loss to predict whether the label is IsNext or NotNext. The [CLS] symbol stands for 'class' and always sits at the start of the sequence, while [SEP] stands for 'separator' and

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: for 'class' and always sits at the start of the sequence, while [SEP] stands for 'separator' and marks the boundary between segments. In addition to token and positional embeddings, each token carries a segment embedding, a zero-or-one value that indicates which of the two segments it belongs to, so the model can tell the two sentences apart when it reads the pair.

metadata.section_title: Next sentence prediction: architecture and the [CLS] token
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT represents text using a WordPiece vocabulary of about thirty thousand common sub-word units (Wu et al., 2016). Sub-word tokenisation lets the model keep common words whole while breaking rare words, spelling variations, misspellings and novel items into smaller pieces; for example 'Transformerify' is split into 'Transformer' and '##ify', where the double-hash marks a continuation piece. This keeps the vocabulary small while still covering any input, including words never

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: continuation piece. This keeps the vocabulary small while still covering any input, including words never seen during training. The final input representation for each position is the sum of three embeddings: a token embedding, a segment embedding that separates the two segments, and a position embedding that encodes word order. Adding these three vectors together gives the input that is fed into the encoder at every position.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT was released in two main sizes. BERT-base has twelve Transformer layers, a hidden size of 768 and twelve attention heads, giving about one hundred million parameters, and was deliberately configured to match OpenAI GPT for comparison. BERT-large has twenty-four layers, a hidden size of 1024 and sixteen attention heads, giving about three hundred and forty million parameters. The models were pre-trained on a corpus combining English Wikipedia, about 2.5 billion words,

metadata.section_title: BERT model configurations and training setup
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: parameters. The models were pre-trained on a corpus combining English Wikipedia, about 2.5 billion words, with BooksCorpus, about 0.8 billion words; by contrast OpenAI GPT was trained on BooksCorpus only. The maximum input length is 512 word pieces. Training ran for one million steps with a batch size of 128,000.

metadata.section_title: BERT model configurations and training setup
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT's two objectives, masked language modelling and next sentence prediction, are trained together in a single pass rather than in separate stages. The representation at the [CLS] position is trained through the next sentence prediction objective, so it learns to summarise the relationship between the two segments. The per-token output representations are trained through masked language modelling, so each token position learns to predict vocabulary items from bidirectional

metadata.section_title: Joint pre-training of MLM and NSP
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: language modelling, so each token position learns to predict vocabulary items from bidirectional context. Sharing one encoder between both objectives means the same network simultaneously learns sentence-level structure, captured at the [CLS] token, and token-level structure, captured at the individual positions.

metadata.section_title: Joint pre-training of MLM and NSP
metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT is evaluated on a range of sentence-level classification tasks, which fall into two groups. Sentence-pair classification takes two sentences as input. In MNLI a premise such as 'A soccer game with multiple males playing' is paired with a hypothesis such as 'Some men are playing a sport' and the model chooses among entailment, contradiction and neutral. In QQP two questions such as 'Where can I learn to invest in stocks?' and 'How can I learn more about stocks?' are

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: questions such as 'Where can I learn to invest in stocks?' and 'How can I learn more about stocks?' are labelled duplicate or not duplicate. Single-sentence classification takes one input; in SST-2 a movie-review fragment like 'rich veins of funny stuff in this movie' is labelled positive or negative. Many of these tasks are collected in the GLUE benchmark (Wang et al., 2018), which contains six sentence-pair tasks and two single-sentence tasks.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT follows a 'pretrain once, fine-tune many times' recipe. For sentence-level tasks the pre-trained encoder is adapted by adding a small task-specific layer on top. For sentence-pair tasks such as MNLI, QQP, QNLI, STS-B, MRPC, RTE and SWAG, the two inputs are joined with a [SEP] token and distinguished by their segment embeddings. A task-specific linear classifier is then placed on top of the [CLS] representation to produce the class label. Single-sentence classification

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: placed on top of the [CLS] representation to produce the class label. Single-sentence classification tasks such as SST-2 and CoLA work the same way but with only one input segment. Because the heavy encoder is already pre-trained, only light task-specific parameters need to be learned during fine-tuning, which is what makes adapting BERT to a new task cheap.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT also supports token-level tasks, where a prediction is needed for individual tokens rather than the whole sentence. One example is extractive question answering, as in the SQuAD dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), where given a question such as which stadium the New York Giants and Jets play at, together with a context paragraph, the model must select the answer span, here 'MetLife Stadium'. Another example is named entity recognition, as in the CoNLL-2003 task (Tjong Kim

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: 'MetLife Stadium'. Another example is named entity recognition, as in the CoNLL-2003 task (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003), where each token is tagged; for the sentence 'John Smith lives in New York' the tags are B-PER, I-PER, O, O, B-LOC and I-LOC, marking the person and location spans.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: For token-level tasks BERT is fine-tuned by adding a task-specific linear classifier on top of the hidden representation of each token, rather than only on the [CLS] position. In extractive question answering on SQuAD the question and paragraph are fed in together separated by [SEP], and the model predicts start and end positions that mark the answer span within the paragraph. In single-sentence tagging such as CoNLL-2003 named entity recognition, each token's hidden vector

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: single-sentence tagging such as CoNLL-2003 named entity recognition, each token's hidden vector is classified into a tag such as O or B-PER. As with sentence-level tasks, the same pre-trained encoder is reused and only a lightweight per-token classifier is added on top.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: An ablation study on model size shows that larger BERT models perform better. As the number of layers, the hidden size and the number of attention heads increase, the language-model perplexity on the development set falls and downstream development-set accuracy on MNLI-m, MRPC and SST-2 rises. For example the smallest configuration with three layers, hidden size 768 and twelve heads reaches about 77.9 on MNLI-m, while the largest with twenty-four layers, hidden size 1024 and

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: heads reaches about 77.9 on MNLI-m, while the largest with twenty-four layers, hidden size 1024 and sixteen heads reaches about 86.6, with MRPC and SST-2 improving in step. The overall message is that, within the range studied, bigger models are consistently better.

metadata.lecture_title: BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers

page_content: BERT sits within a broader trend of rapidly growing language models. Charting models by parameter count and by training-corpus size shows a steep climb from ELMo and BERT through the GPT family, with GPT-3 far larger than its predecessors in both parameters and tokens seen. page_content: Natural language processing often works as a pipeline of components, where each component adds a further layer of structure to raw, unstructured text. A typical pipeline begins with sentence segmentation, which takes a block of text and splits it into individual sentences. Tokenisation then takes each sentence and breaks it into tokens. Part-of-speech tagging takes those tokens and assigns a POS tag to each one. Parsing takes the tagged tokens and produces dependency

page_content: tokens and assigns a POS tag to each one. Parsing takes the tagged tokens and produces dependency structure, and relation extraction finally turns those dependencies into structured relations that can be stored and queried. Because the stages are arranged in sequence, later components depend heavily on the quality of the earlier ones: an error in tokenisation or tagging propagates downstream and can corrupt parsing and extraction. Moving from unstructured text on the left to

page_content: downstream and can corrupt parsing and extraction. Moving from unstructured text on the left to structured relations on the right is the overall goal of the pipeline.

page_content: Parts of speech are classes of words defined by their grammatical role in a sentence. Open classes such as nouns (house, health, London), verbs (walks, gave, showing), adjectives (small, better) and adverbs (almost, happily) carry much of the descriptive content and readily admit new members. Closed classes such as pronouns (he, they), determiners (the, a, an), conjunctions (and, or, because) and prepositions (in, of, from) are small, stable sets of function words. Assigning

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: or, because) and prepositions (in, of, from) are small, stable sets of function words. Assigning a part of speech to a word describes how that word functions within its sentence rather than what it means in isolation. POS tags therefore give us a compact vocabulary for talking about grammatical behaviour, and they form the categorical foundation that later stages such as parsing build upon.

page_content: POS tags come from standard annotation schemes, and two schemes are especially common. The Penn Treebank tagset is detailed and English-focused, with fine distinctions such as NN for a singular or mass noun, NNS for a plural noun, NNP for a singular proper noun, VBD for a past-tense verb, VBZ for a third-person singular present verb, JJ for an adjective and DT for a determiner, plus further tags for punctuation. The Universal POS tagset is broader and cross-linguistic,

page_content: determiner, plus further tags for punctuation. The Universal POS tagset is broader and cross-linguistic, grouping words into open-class categories (ADJ, ADV, INTJ, NOUN, PROPN, VERB), closed-class categories (ADP, AUX, CCONJ, DET, NUM, PART, PRON, SCONJ) and an other group (PUNCT, SYM, X). The same proper noun that Penn Treebank labels NNP is labelled PROPN under the Universal scheme; a past-tense verb tagged VBD maps to VERB, and a determiner tagged DT maps to DET. Choosing

page_content: scheme; a past-tense verb tagged VBD maps to VERB, and a determiner tagged DT maps to DET. Choosing a scheme is a trade-off between English-specific detail and cross-language comparability.

page_content: The part-of-speech tagging task is to assign exactly one POS tag to each token in a sentence. Tagging usually happens after tokenisation, so its input is the sequence of tokens produced by the tokeniser and its output is a parallel sequence of tags. For example, in 'Book that flight.' the word Book is tagged VB, that is DT, flight is NN and the full stop is punctuation, whereas in 'Does that flight serve dinner?' the verb Does is tagged VBZ. A crucial property of the task is

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: 'Does that flight serve dinner?' the verb Does is tagged VBZ. A crucial property of the task is that the same word can receive different tags in different contexts, so tagging is a token-level classification problem in which the surrounding tokens, not just the word itself, determine the answer.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: Part-of-speech tagging is hard because many words are ambiguous when seen in isolation. Some ambiguity is lexical: the word duck can be a verb meaning an action or a noun naming a bird, and referee can be a verb (they referee the matches) or a noun (the referee starts the match). Other ambiguity comes from a word taking different syntactic roles, as in 'to walk' versus 'go for a walk', or 'old people' versus 'the old'. Because a single surface form can belong to several

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: for a walk', or 'old people' versus 'the old'. Because a single surface form can belong to several categories, tagging in a great many cases is really a disambiguation task: the tagger must decide which of the possible tags is correct for this particular occurrence.

page_content: Local context often makes the correct tag much clearer, because ambiguity that appears when a token stands alone frequently disappears once the token is placed beside its neighbours. After a determiner a word is very unlikely to be a verb, so in 'I want a go' the word go is read as a noun, while after the word to a word is unlikely to be a noun, so in 'I want to go' the word go is read as a verb. Similarly 'a walk' suggests a noun and 'to walk' suggests a verb, and in 'the

page_content: is read as a verb. Similarly 'a walk' suggests a noun and 'to walk' suggests a verb, and in 'the old man' the word old is an adjective. A token is also more likely to be a possessive pronoun when it is followed by a common noun, as in 'he stroked her cat'. These regularities are only tendencies rather than certainties, since 'he gave her money' shows the same word her behaving differently, and 'they can fish' stays ambiguous even in context. page_content: behaving differently, and 'they can fish' stays ambiguous even in context. POS tagging models learn how neighbouring words influence the likely tag.

page_content: Meaning affects tagging, so a single sentence can have more than one valid tag sequence depending on what it is understood to mean. Take 'I saw her duck.': if it means the speaker saw her pet bird, then duck is a NOUN, but if it means the speaker saw her lower her head quickly, then duck is a VERB, with the rest of the sentence tagged identically as PRON, VERB and PRON. The tagger must choose the tag that matches the intended meaning. The task still assigns only one POS tag

page_content: tagger must choose the tag that matches the intended meaning. The task still assigns only one POS tag per token for each run, and different readings correspond to different runs. In 'They can fish', one run tags can as AUX and fish as VERB, while another tags can as VERB and fish as NOUN; likewise 'I saw her bat' can end in NOUN or VERB.

page_content: Two broad families of approaches perform POS tagging. A rule-based approach uses handcrafted grammatical rules written by experts. A statistical or neural approach instead learns patterns from annotated corpora. POS-tagged corpora are valuable because they supply example sentences, gold labels for each token, and concrete evidence for disambiguation that a model can learn from. One way to label a new sentence is autoregressive prediction, which uses the previous token and its

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: way to label a new sentence is autoregressive prediction, which uses the previous token and its tag as context to help generate the tag for the current token. In practice modern tagging systems are usually data-driven, because learning from large labelled corpora generalises better than maintaining large collections of hand-written rules.

page_content: A POS-tagged corpus stores each token beside its gold tag, and the same sentences can be annotated under different schemes. Under the Penn Treebank scheme the sentence 'Today is a nice day.' is tagged Today/NN is/VBZ a/DT nice/JJ day/NN with a final punctuation tag, and 'I want to go for a walk.' is tagged I/PRP want/VBP to/TO go/VB for/IN a/DT walk/NN. page_content: POS tags tell us the category of each word, but syntactic parsing tells us how the words are structurally related to one another. Parsing helps answer questions that categories alone cannot, such as which noun is the subject, which phrase is the object, and what a prepositional phrase modifies. There are two major views of syntax that parsing can express. Dependency structure describes the sentence as a set of directed grammatical relations between words. Phrase structure

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: describes the sentence as a set of directed grammatical relations between words. Phrase structure describes the sentence as words grouped into nested constituents. Both views go beyond a flat list of POS tags by making the relationships among words explicit.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: Parsing matters because some sentences remain ambiguous even after every word has been tagged. In 'The teacher discussed the essay with the student', the phrase 'with the student' might describe who the teacher talked to, or it might describe which essay was discussed, and POS tags alone cannot settle the question. Parsing makes such structural choices explicit. Some sentences also allow more than one syntactic analysis, so that the same sequence of words produces different

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: also allow more than one syntactic analysis, so that the same sequence of words produces different structures and therefore different meanings. To understand a sentence we cannot treat each word in isolation; we must determine what each word is attached or connected to.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: Syntactic ambiguity arises when the same string of words supports more than one grammatical structure. 'I saw the man on the hill with a telescope' can be read with the telescope belonging to the seeing or to the man, and 'The violent policeman injures the farmer with an ax' has the same kind of prepositional uncertainty. 'Flying planes can be dangerous' and 'Visiting relatives can be boring' are ambiguous because the leading phrase can be understood in two ways. The lesson

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: can be boring' are ambiguous because the leading phrase can be understood in two ways. The lesson is that to understand sentences we cannot treat each word in isolation; we need to determine what a word is attached or connected to, which is precisely the information a parse provides.

page_content: A dependency parse represents grammatical relations between words. Every relation links two words: a head and a dependent, where the dependent attaches to and is governed by its head. The head of the whole sentence is usually the main verb. Taken together the relations form a directed structure over the tokens, in which arrows run from heads to their dependents and each labelled edge names the grammatical function involved, such as a determiner (det) relation linking a

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: labelled edge names the grammatical function involved, such as a determiner (det) relation linking a determiner to the noun it depends on. This word-to-word view contrasts with phrase structure, which instead groups words into constituents rather than linking them directly.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: In dependency parsing the sentence head is often the main predicate, and it acts as the root of the analysis. Subjects and objects depend on that predicate, while modifiers depend on the specific word they modify. In 'The child opened the door', the verb opened is the root of the sentence, child is a subject dependent of opened, and door is an object dependent of opened. Reading a parse therefore begins by finding the root and then asking which words depend directly on it and

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: parse therefore begins by finding the root and then asking which words depend directly on it and in what role, which reveals the backbone of the sentence before the smaller modifying relations are considered.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: In a dependency analysis one token acts as the structural centre of the sentence, and the other words connect to it through grammatical relations such as subject, object and modifier. The labels on the edges tell us how each token functions, which makes the sentence structure explicit and easier to analyse. In 'Economic news had little effect on financial markets', the verb had is the root; news is its subject (sbj) and effect is its object (obj); Economic modifies news and

page_content: is the root; news is its subject (sbj) and effect is its object (obj); Economic modifies news and little and on modify effect through nominal-modifier (nmod) relations; and the preposition on takes markets as its object (pc), with financial modifying markets. To read such a parse, ask what the root is, which words depend directly on the root, which words modify nouns, and which phrases modify the event.

page_content: Dependency schemes use a labelled inventory of relations, and several labels appear repeatedly. A nominal subject (nsubj or sbj) links a verb to the noun phrase that serves as its subject, as in sbj(defeated, Clinton). An object (obj or dobj) links a verb to the noun phrase acted upon, and an indirect object (iobj) marks a recipient, as in iobj(gave, me). Nominal and adjectival modifiers (nmod or amod) modify a noun phrase, as in nmod(meat, red), while a verb modifier (vmod)

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: modifiers (nmod or amod) modify a noun phrase, as in nmod(meat, red), while a verb modifier (vmod) modifies a verb phrase. A determiner relation (det) links the head of a noun phrase to its determiner, as in det(man, the); an auxiliary relation (aux) marks a non-main verb, as in aux(leave, should); coordination (cc) connects a conjunct to a coordinating word; an object of preposition (pobj or pc) is the head of the noun phrase following a preposition; and punctuation (p or

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: preposition (pobj or pc) is the head of the noun phrase following a preposition; and punctuation (p or punct) links the root to punctuation. The exact inventory depends on the annotation scheme.

page_content: A major challenge in parsing is attachment ambiguity, where a phrase could legitimately attach to more than one earlier word. Consider 'The teacher discussed the essay with the student.' Under one interpretation the phrase 'with the student' modifies the verb discussed, meaning the teacher talked to the student. Under another interpretation the same phrase modifies the noun essay, meaning the essay is about or associated with the student. Each reading corresponds to a

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: essay, meaning the essay is about or associated with the student. Each reading corresponds to a different parse, because the phrase attaches to a different head. Different meanings therefore require different parses, and choosing the right attachment is one of the central problems a parser must solve.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: To decide where a phrase attaches, ask which word the phrase is modifying. If the phrase describes the event or action being reported, it usually attaches to the verb, whereas if the phrase describes an entity such as a person or object, it usually attaches to the noun that names that entity. Because this decision depends on what the sentence is understood to be about, parsing is closely tied to semantic interpretation: resolving an attachment is often as much a question of

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: closely tied to semantic interpretation: resolving an attachment is often as much a question of meaning as of grammar, and the two cannot be fully separated.

page_content: Phrase structure parsing represents a sentence as nested constituents. Instead of drawing head-dependent links between individual words, it groups words together into phrases and then groups those phrases into larger phrases. Typical phrase types include the noun phrase (NP), the verb phrase (VP), the prepositional phrase (PP), the adjectival phrase (AdjP) and the adverbial phrase (AdvP). Because constituents nest inside one another, the analysis forms a hierarchy that runs

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: phrase (AdvP). Because constituents nest inside one another, the analysis forms a hierarchy that runs from the whole sentence (S) at the top down to the individual tagged words at the leaves, showing how small groups combine into progressively larger ones.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: Building a phrase structure tree usually proceeds in stages, and the result shows both grouping and hierarchy. First, label the syntactic category of each token, so that in 'The child put the puppy in the garden' the tags are DT NN VBD DT NN IN DT NN. Second, locate the boundary between the two principal constituents, a noun phrase and a verb phrase, giving [The child] [put the puppy in the garden]. Third, for each head noun, verb, adjective, adverb and preposition, project a

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: puppy in the garden]. Third, for each head noun, verb, adjective, adverb and preposition, project a phrasal node such as NP, VP, AdjP, AdvP or PP. Fourth, connect the remaining tokens to the nodes they belong to. Finally, combine the phrases under a single sentence node S to complete the tree.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: A noun phrase is centred on a noun or pronoun and may contain additional material that belongs with that head. It can include determiners, adjectives, possessives and modifiers, so 'the child', 'her old bicycle' and 'the report on climate change' are all noun phrases even though they differ in length and internal make-up. Recognising a noun phrase means finding its head noun and the words that group around it, not simply grabbing a long run of words. Not every long span in a

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: the words that group around it, not simply grabbing a long run of words. Not every long span in a sentence is a noun phrase, so the grouping must respect where the constituent actually begins and ends.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: Dependency parsing and phrase structure parsing offer complementary views. Dependency parsing focuses on relations between words and is especially useful for predicate-argument structure, information extraction and relation analysis. Phrase structure parsing focuses on constituent groupings and is especially useful for constituent identification, NP, VP and PP analysis, and hierarchical sentence structure. They also differ in what each representation can encode. A dependency

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: hierarchical sentence structure. They also differ in what each representation can encode. A dependency structure uses directed head-dependent edges, edge labels for grammatical functions, and POS tags for syntactic categories. A phrase structure uses non-terminal nodes for phrases and their hierarchy, together with POS tags for syntactic categories, but it does not label word-to-word grammatical functions directly.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: Dependency constructions can be classified by whether the dependent is required. In an exocentric construction the dependent is obligatory: a verb requires its subject (sbj) and a verb requires its object (obj), so removing them breaks the construction. In an endocentric construction the dependent is optional: a verb does not require an adverbial modifier (vmod) and a noun does not require an adjectival modifier (nmod), so these dependents can be dropped while the head still

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: not require an adjectival modifier (nmod), so these dependents can be dropped while the head still stands on its own. Endocentric dependents are therefore sometimes optional, which distinguishes them from the required arguments found in exocentric constructions.

page_content: The same dependency analysis can be drawn in several notations, which differ in appearance rather than in content. One notation arranges the tokens horizontally and draws directed edges above and below them, labelling each edge with its grammatical function such as sbj, obj, nmod, pc and p. A second notation looks identical but reverses the direction of the arrows, so the reader must check which way heads and dependents point. A third notation redraws the analysis as a tree

page_content: must check which way heads and dependents point. A third notation redraws the analysis as a tree of tokens, placing the root at the top. A fourth notation draws a tree of POS tags mapped to their tokens, combining tokens, grammatical functions and POS tags in one picture. There are far too many notations to memorise, but they are just formalisms, and the same conceptual similarities appear across all of them.

page_content: Named Entity Recognition, or NER, identifies mentions of real-world entities in text and assigns a label to each mention. Typical entity types include person, organisation, location, date or time, and money. NER helps answer practical questions about a document, such as who is mentioned, where something happened, and which organisations are involved. In a news snippet, for instance, a briefing location, a time expression, a named politician and a named vaccine group could

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: instance, a briefing location, a time expression, a named politician and a named vaccine group could each be picked out and labelled with its type. By turning free text into a list of typed mentions, NER provides a first structured summary of the people, places and organisations a document is about.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: The set of useful entity types depends on the application domain, so NER does not have one fixed universal label set. In news text the common types are person, organisation, location and date. In biomedical text a different inventory is more useful, including drug, disease, protein and virus, because those are the categories that matter for reading scientific literature. A biomedical passage might therefore label a drug or chemical, a gene or protein, a virus and a disease,

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: biomedical passage might therefore label a drug or chemical, a gene or protein, a virus and a disease, none of which appear in a typical news schema. Choosing the entity types is thus part of defining the task rather than something fixed in advance.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: NER is context-dependent because the same string can refer to different entity types in different contexts. The word Washington may refer to a person, to a city, or to a government, and the word Amazon may refer to a company or to a river, with only the surrounding text revealing which reading is intended. For this reason NER systems must use context rather than relying on the surface form of a word alone. A system that memorised a fixed label for each string would fail on

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: surface form of a word alone. A system that memorised a fixed label for each string would fail on exactly these cases, so contextual evidence is essential for assigning the correct type.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: A common way to formulate NER is as a token-level sequence labelling task, in which every token receives a tag. That tag records two things at once: whether the token is inside an entity, and if so which entity type it belongs to. This makes NER closely resemble POS tagging, since both assign a label to each token in order. The important addition in NER is that the tags must also encode span boundaries, so that a system can tell where one multi-word entity ends and the next

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: encode span boundaries, so that a system can tell where one multi-word entity ends and the next begins rather than only categorising isolated words.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: The BIO tagging scheme encodes entity spans through three kinds of token tag. A B-X tag marks the beginning of an entity of type X, an I-X tag marks a token that is inside an entity of type X, and an O tag marks a token that is outside any entity. For example, 'Maya Chen works at Northbridge Labs in Leeds.' is tagged B-PER I-PER O O B-ORG I-ORG O B-LOC O, so that Maya Chen forms a two-token person entity and Northbridge Labs forms a two-token organisation entity. Consecutive

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: two-token person entity and Northbridge Labs forms a two-token organisation entity. Consecutive BIO tags define complete mentions: a B-PER followed by an I-PER is read as one two-token person entity. BIO therefore lets us recover entity spans from token-level labels, and a correct prediction needs both the correct span and the correct type.

The reasoning is that each type contributes one B tag for its beginning and one I tag for its interior, giving 2N type-specific tags, and a single shared O tag is added for tokens outside any entity. For the three types person, organisation and location, the classes are B-PER, I-PER, B-ORG, I-ORG, B-LOC and I-LOC together with O, which is seven classes in total, matching 2 times 3 plus 1.

page_content: Sequence models for NER can be local or global. A local model predicts each tag mainly from token-level context and treats the output tags as independent of one another, so any sequence classifier such as an RNN, an LSTM or a BiLSTM can be used. A global model instead predicts a whole label sequence while considering dependencies between the output tags, as in a Hidden Markov Model or a Conditional Random Field. This distinction matters because some tag sequences are far more

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: or a Conditional Random Field. This distinction matters because some tag sequences are far more plausible than others: for example, an I-ORG tag should not normally appear directly after an O tag without a preceding B-ORG, and only a model that reasons about tag-to-tag transitions can rule such sequences out.

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: A Conditional Random Field, or CRF, is a global sequence model that scores an entire output sequence rather than scoring each token independently. Because it considers the whole sequence, a CRF can model dependencies such as which BIO transitions are legal and how neighbouring labels should stay consistent, which often improves sequence-labelling performance. In a linear-chain CRF the probability of a label sequence given the input is computed as a normalised exponential of a

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: the probability of a label sequence given the input is computed as a normalised exponential of a sum, over all tokens and all feature functions, of each feature function's value weighted by its learned weight, where each feature function depends on the current label, the previous label and the current input. A normalisation factor, summed over all possible label sequences, ensures the probabilities add up to one.

page_content: Classical NER models often rely on handcrafted features computed for each token. Contextual features include the current word and the surrounding words in a window, and the part-of-speech tag when it is available. Orthographic features capture the shape of a word, such as initial capitals, all-capitals, all-digits, whether it contains dots or a hyphen, whether it is a single character or a URL, and whether it is a Roman numeral. Prefixes and suffixes of length one to four are

metadata.lecture_title: Sequence Labeling and Evaluations in Text Mining

page_content: character or a URL, and whether it is a Roman numeral. Prefixes and suffixes of length one to four are taken from each component and from the whole entity. Trigger words signal likely types, such as titles like Mr, Miss, Dr, PhD or Prof for a person, words like city or street for a location, and endings like Ltd or Co for an organisation. Common architectures include the BiLSTM, the BiLSTM-CRF, which adds a CRF layer on top to model tag transitions, and Transformer-based encoders. A recurrent network is used so that the hidden representation of each token reflects its surrounding context. These models often perform well when sufficient training data is available.
