page_content: The examinable material is organised into five high-yield clusters. The first cluster is Transformers and representations, covering the comparison with RNNs, positional encoding, attention, embeddings and TF-IDF. The second is LLM training and adaptation, covering pretraining, instruction tuning, alignment, mixture-of-experts and reasoning models. The third is prompting and applications, covering in-context learning, chain-of-thought, retrieval-augmented generation, agents,

applications, covering in-context learning, chain-of-thought, retrieval-augmented generation, agents, multimodal systems and safety. The fourth is sequence labelling, covering POS tagging, dependency parsing, phrase structure and named-entity recognition with the BIO scheme. The fifth is evaluation, covering gold standards, Cohen's kappa, precision, recall and F1, averaging methods and entity-level scoring.

Transformers differ from RNN sequence-to-sequence models in several ways that the exam tends to test as conceptual distinctions. An RNN processes tokens sequentially, one position after another, whereas a Transformer processes all input positions in parallel. In an RNN the context is often bottlenecked through the hidden state, although attention mechanisms can help; a Transformer instead uses dynamic self-attention over all positions at once. Long-range dependencies are

Transformer instead uses dynamic self-attention over all positions at once. Long-range dependencies are harder for an RNN because information must pass through many recurrent steps, while a Transformer has direct pairwise attention paths between any two positions. Order information is implicit in an RNN's recurrence, but a Transformer has no recurrence, so it needs positional information to be added explicitly. A key point for answers: Transformers do not use recurrence, and

information to be added explicitly. A key point for answers: Transformers do not use recurrence, and self-attention lets each token build context by attending to other tokens while positional encodings supply order. A common trap is to claim Transformers ignore word order entirely; in fact they model order once positional information has been added.

Self-attention on its own treats positions symmetrically, so a plain attention layer cannot tell where a token sits in the sequence; order has to be injected. This is done by adding position vectors to the token embeddings to produce order-aware representations. There are two main styles. Sinusoidal positional encodings are a fixed function of position, are not learned, and can in principle extrapolate to longer sequences by formula; they are part of the classic Transformer

in principle extrapolate to longer sequences by formula; they are part of the classic Transformer design. Learned positional encodings are trainable vectors updated together with the model weights and are common in many modern systems, but they are limited by the context length seen during training. The exam may ask you to identify correct statements about why positional encodings are needed and whether they are learned. The intuition: without positional encodings, sentences

are needed and whether they are learned. The intuition: without positional encodings, sentences like 'dogs chase cats' and 'cats chase dogs' are hard for plain self-attention because it lacks an explicit signal for token order.

Multi-head attention runs several attention heads in parallel. The input representations are projected into queries, keys and values, several attention heads each compute their own attention, the head outputs are concatenated, and a final output projection is applied. The core idea is that each head attends using its own learned query, key and value projections, so different heads can focus on different representation subspaces or different kinds of relations in the same

heads can focus on different representation subspaces or different kinds of relations in the same sequence. A common dimension rule sets d_head = d_model / h, so with d_model = 768 and h = 12 heads each head has dimension 64; after concatenation the output returns to d_model before the output projection. A frequent trap is to think that heads are separate slices of the input sequence, but they are not. Every head processes the same sequence, just through different learned
sequence, but they are not. Every head processes the same sequence, just through different learned projections.

There are three Transformer architecture families, and the exam expects you to know the attention pattern, typical use case and example models of each. Encoder-only models such as BERT and RoBERTa use bidirectional self-attention and are best for natural-language understanding tasks like classification, tagging and extraction; they are often pretrained with masked-language-modelling objectives. Encoder-decoder models such as T5 and BART use an encoder to represent the input

masked-language-modelling objectives. Encoder-decoder models such as T5 and BART use an encoder to represent the input and a decoder to generate output, where the decoder combines self-attention with cross-attention to the encoder output. Decoder-only models such as GPT-style LLMs use causal masked self-attention, so prompt understanding and generation happen in a single left-to-right stream. Three things to remember: BERT is not autoregressive, T5 uses cross-attention, and
left-to-right stream. Three things to remember: BERT is not autoregressive, T5 uses cross-attention, and GPT relies on causal masking.

Word representations can be compared with cosine similarity, defined as the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their norms: cosine of A and B equals A dot B divided by the product of the norm of A and the norm of B. Count-based vectors come from term-document or term-term matrices; they are high-dimensional and sparse, store one vector per word type, and can be expensive to hold in memory. TF-IDF weighting down-weights very common terms and emphasises

can be expensive to hold in memory. TF-IDF weighting down-weights very common terms and emphasises informative ones, but it does not by itself remove sparsity. Static vectors also struggle with polysemy, because one vector must represent all senses of a word, whereas contextual models can represent the same word differently in different sentences. A worked example: for A equal to one, one, zero and B equal to one, zero, zero the dot product is one and the norms are root two
one, one, zero and B equal to one, zero, zero the dot product is one and the norms are root two and one, so the cosine similarity is about 0.71.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, answers a user query by first retrieving relevant evidence and then generating a grounded answer. The flow is: the user query goes to a retriever, which searches a knowledge source such as an external corpus or vector database, returns retrieved passages, and passes them with the query to a generator LLM, which produces the grounded answer. The essential parts are an external corpus or vector database, a retriever, a generator, and a

answer. The essential parts are an external corpus or vector database, a retriever, a generator, and a prompt that combines the query with the retrieved evidence. RAG is the right choice when facts change often, when large private documents must be consulted, when you need citation-like grounding, or when fine-tuning would be too expensive or inappropriate. It should not be confused with pretraining from scratch, with supervised fine-tuning on a handbook alone, or with a

confused with pretraining from scratch, with supervised fine-tuning on a handbook alone, or with a model simply guessing from its parametric memory. For example, a company question-and-answer bot that must answer from a changing policy manual is usually best served by an instruction-tuned LLM combined with RAG.

LLM pretraining predicts the next token in raw text. Text is tokenised, the model predicts the next token, a cross-entropy loss compares the prediction to the actual next token, and the weights are updated. It is self-supervised: no manual labels are required because the next token in the text itself supplies the training target. It helps to separate training from inference. During training the model compares its prediction to the ground-truth next token and updates weights;

During training the model compares its prediction to the ground-truth next token and updates weights; during inference it chooses or samples the next token and feeds it back in autoregressively. Formally the sequence probability factorises autoregressively as the product over positions of the probability of each token given the tokens before it. An important limitation is that this objective optimises likelihood, not truth, so models may hallucinate, repeat biases, or
that this objective optimises likelihood, not truth, so models may hallucinate, repeat biases, or generate unsafe content.

After pretraining, models are adapted in stages, and the exam tends to ask what each stage changes and what it does not guarantee. Pretraining does general language modelling from raw text. Instruction tuning, also called supervised fine-tuning, teaches the model to follow natural-language instructions using instruction-response pairs. RLHF and other preference-optimisation methods shift behaviour toward human preferences and safety, and DPO, PPO and GRPO are different

methods shift behaviour toward human preferences and safety, and DPO, PPO and GRPO are different optimisation routes for that preference alignment. The target behaviour is often summarised as HHH: helpful, meaning it answers the task; honest, meaning it says what is known and unknown; and harmless, meaning it avoids unsafe or abusive outputs. A common trap is to treat instruction tuning as the same as RLHF: instruction tuning is supervised and may be followed by RLHF. Another

tuning as the same as RLHF: instruction tuning is supervised and may be followed by RLHF. Another trap is to assume instruction tuning guarantees factual accuracy; it improves instruction-following and zero-shot or few-shot behaviour, but it does not guarantee that answers are factually correct.

A Mixture of Experts, or MoE, has several expert networks that share a model, with a gating or router network that selects one or a few experts for each token. The token state goes to a router, which picks among experts and combines their outputs. The advantages are sparse activation, faster pretraining and easier scaling, because only a subset of experts runs per token; the costs are greater complexity, higher memory use, and fine-tuning challenges. Sparse activation

page_content: the costs are greater complexity, higher memory use, and fine-tuning challenges. Sparse activation specifically means that only a subset of the experts is active for any given token rather than the whole network. Reasoning models are a separate idea: they allocate more test-time compute by generating intermediate reasoning before the final response. The trade-off is that a smaller model that thinks for longer can sometimes beat a larger model that answers immediately, but

page_content: smaller model that thinks for longer can sometimes beat a larger model that answers immediately, but latency and cost increase.

page_content: A well-formed prompt usually has four components. The instruction states what task the model should do. The context supplies the role, constraints and background. The input data is the actual text, table, image description or query to work on. The output indicator specifies the desired format, such as labels, a JSON schema or bullet points. Good practice includes using clear delimiters around user data, specifying the exact output format, preferring positive instructions,

delimiters around user data, specifying the exact output format, preferring positive instructions, giving examples for custom formats, and checking for prompt injection. The exam may show a vague prompt such as 'Analyse this' and ask you to make it exam-ready by adding an explicit instruction, context, a delimited input and an output format; more specific prompts reduce ambiguity.

In-context learning, or ICL, is about giving examples in the prompt rather than updating model weights. In zero-shot mode the model receives an instruction plus the target input with no examples. In one- or few-shot mode it receives the instruction, one to five demonstrations, and the target input. Fine-tuning, by contrast, uses training data to update weights. The key point about ICL is that it involves no gradient descent; it uses temporary working memory only. It helps to

ICL is that it involves no gradient descent; it uses temporary working memory only. It helps to contrast two kinds of memory: parametric memory is the knowledge stored in the model weights learned during training, while working memory is the current prompt or context window. So a prompt that shows a couple of translated example pairs before asking for a new translation is using ICL, because it provides demonstrations in the prompt without changing any weights.

Several prompting strategies encourage reasoning, and the exam may ask which is safest or most appropriate. Chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate reasoning before the answer and is useful for multi-step maths, logic and planning; a short trigger phrase can help, but chain-of-thought is not a calculator. Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning paths and takes a majority vote over their answers, and Tree of Thoughts explores branches and backtracks. Prompt

majority vote over their answers, and Tree of Thoughts explores branches and backtracks. Prompt injection is a security concern: because instructions and data are both just text, malicious user content can try to override the intended task, so you should separate instructions from data and validate any tool use. For exact arithmetic inside an agent it is safer to call an external calculator or Python tool and return the observation than to rely on pure chain-of-thought.

LLMs support a range of applications. Core NLP tasks include summarisation, structured extraction and named-entity recognition, classification and routing, and question answering. Domain applications include code work such as writing unit tests and fixing bugs, legal and finance work that uses RAG for current facts, and healthcare, which requires strict human review. An agent has four parts: the LLM as its brain, memory in the form of a context or vector store, tools such as

four parts: the LLM as its brain, memory in the form of a context or vector store, tools such as APIs, a calculator or a browser, and a loop that plans, acts and observes. Deployment bottlenecks include inference cost, latency, probabilistic reliability, monitoring, safety, prompt injection, and copyright or intellectual-property concerns. For instance, a legal assistant that must answer from a changing database of cases is best built with RAG plus careful evaluation and
must answer from a changing database of cases is best built with RAG plus careful evaluation and human review rather than prompting alone or pretraining from scratch.

Multimodal LLMs combine a modality encoder with a language model. An image or audio input passes through a modality encoder, then a connector or projection layer, then the LLM backbone, which produces text or action output. Architecturally this means a vision encoder or audio encoder, a projection layer sometimes called a Q-Former, and the LLM that performs the complex reasoning and generation. Evaluation raises a specific issue: exact string matching can penalise chatty but

and generation. Evaluation raises a specific issue: exact string matching can penalise chatty but correct answers, so modern multimodal evaluation often uses rubric-based scoring or an LLM-as-judge. Hallucination is another concern: the model may describe objects or relations that are absent from the image, driven by language priors or by compressed visual tokens. That is why a visual-question-answering system might answer 'chair' near a table even when no chair is visible.

Part-of-speech tagging assigns one POS tag to each token after tokenisation, and the same word can take different tags in different contexts. Two tagsets appear frequently. The Penn Treebank tagset is detailed and English-focused. The Universal POS tagset uses broader cross-linguistic categories such as PRON, AUX, VERB, NOUN, DET and PUNCT. To decide a tag, use the local context and the intended meaning and ask whether the token is acting as a noun, verb, auxiliary,

context and the intended meaning and ask whether the token is acting as a noun, verb, auxiliary, determiner and so on. For example, in the sentence 'We watched her duck', the word 'duck' is a NOUN under the reading where it is her pet bird, but a VERB under the reading where she quickly lowers her head. The exam often states the intended meaning and asks you to tag the ambiguous word accordingly.

Dependency parsing represents a sentence as labelled links from a head word to its dependents, with labels such as nsubj for subject, obj for object, and various modifiers. A good reading strategy is to first find the main predicate or root, then identify its direct dependents such as the subject, object and modifiers, then for each modifier ask which word it describes, and finally use meaning to resolve any attachment ambiguity. For the sentence 'The analyst emailed the

finally use meaning to resolve any attachment ambiguity. For the sentence 'The analyst emailed the report to Maria', the root is 'emailed', the subject dependent is 'analyst', the object dependent is 'report', and 'Maria' is the recipient introduced by the prepositional phrase. A common trap is to confuse the preposition itself with the noun it introduces as the semantic head.

Attachment ambiguity happens when the same words can form different structures depending on the intended meaning. Take the sentence 'The reviewer read the article with a chart'. Under one reading, 'with a chart' is an event modifier describing how the reviewer read, so the prepositional phrase attaches to the verb or reading event. Under the other reading, 'with a chart' describes which article, so the prepositional phrase attaches to the noun phrase 'article'. The exam-style

which article, so the prepositional phrase attaches to the noun phrase 'article'. The exam-style method is to first paraphrase the intended meaning and then draw or read the dependency or phrase structure to match it: meaning decides the attachment.

Phrase structure parsing groups words into nested constituents rather than head-dependent arcs, with typical nodes such as S, NP, VP, PP, AdjP and AdvP. A noun phrase is centred on a noun or pronoun and may include determiners, adjectives, possessives and modifiers. Not every span of words is a constituent: a long sequence is not automatically a noun phrase, so you should check whether it has a noun or pronoun head and whether it actually forms a constituent. For example, in

whether it has a noun or pronoun head and whether it actually forms a constituent. For example, in the sentence 'The student from Leeds solved the puzzle', two noun phrases are 'The student from Leeds' and 'the puzzle', and 'Leeds' is itself a noun phrase inside the prepositional phrase.

Named-entity recognition identifies spans that mention real-world entities and assigns a type such as PER, ORG, LOC, DATE or MONEY. The BIO scheme labels tokens so that B-X begins an entity of type X, I-X continues an entity of type X, and O marks a token outside any entity. This gives a simple formula for the number of output classes: for T entity types under BIO you need two T plus one classes, a B- tag and an I- tag for each type plus a single O tag. So a system that

page_content: two T plus one classes, a B- tag and an I- tag for each type plus a single O tag. So a system that recognises PER, ORG, LOC and DATE needs two times four plus one, which is nine classes. Entity-level scoring is strict: both the exact span and the entity type must match, and a token-level partial overlap does not necessarily count as a correct entity.

page_content: Gold standards are reference labels created with annotation guidelines so that a system's responses can be compared against reliable references. Two agreement quantities matter. Observed agreement, written P sub a, is the proportion of items on which the annotators agree, but it does not correct for agreement that could happen by chance. Expected agreement, written P sub e, estimates that chance agreement from the annotators' label distributions. Cohen's kappa combines them

metadata.section_title: Gold standards, agreement, and Cohen's Kappa

page_content: estimates that chance agreement from the annotators' label distributions. Cohen's kappa combines them as kappa equals P sub a minus P sub e, all divided by one minus P sub e, which rewards agreement beyond chance. For example, if P sub a is 0.80 and P sub e is 0.50, then kappa equals 0.80 minus 0.50 over 1 minus 0.50, which is 0.30 divided by 0.50, giving 0.60.

page_content: Precision, recall and F1 are computed from a confusion matrix of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Precision is TP divided by TP plus FP, recall is TP divided by TP plus FN, and F1 is their harmonic mean, two P R divided by P plus R. For example, with TP equal to 3, FP equal to 1 and FN equal to 2, precision is 0.75, recall is 0.60 and F1 is about 0.667. When there are several classes, results can be averaged in different ways: micro

is about 0.667. When there are several classes, results can be averaged in different ways: micro averaging pools the counts across classes, macro averaging averages the per-class scores equally so every class counts the same, and weighted averaging averages by class support. Accuracy can mislead on imbalanced data, which is why precision and recall are preferred. Entity-level scoring for NER requires the exact span and type to match, so a token-level partial overlap is not
scoring for NER requires the exact span and type to match, so a token-level partial overlap is not necessarily a correct entity.

A final revision plan has three parts. First, memorise the formulas: cosine similarity, the ingredients of TF-IDF, Cohen's kappa, precision, recall and F1, the difference between micro and macro averaging, and the BIO class count of two T plus one. Second, practise the skills: select-all conceptual traps, POS tags under a stated meaning, dependency heads and dependents, phrase constituents, exact-match NER counting, and architecture-selection scenarios. Third, avoid common

constituents, exact-match NER counting, and architecture-selection scenarios. Third, avoid common mistakes: treating in-context learning as weight updates, calling instruction tuning a guarantee of factuality, confusing precision and recall, counting partial NER spans as correct, and ignoring the stated sentence interpretation. When unsure, define the task, identify the representation, then compute or reason from the definition.
